description: Existing informational brochures had not been previously evaluated and lacked prior feedback from patients and healthcare professionals, leaving gaps in designers' evidence about acceptability and usability.
justification: This knowledge gap limits the designers' ability to manage user understanding, specify user requirements, and to plan effective evaluation and iteration of the materials before wider implementation.
reference_excerpt: The effectiveness of the brochures created so far has not been tested, and there is no hindsight or feedback from patients or healthcare professionals regarding their acceptability, usability and usefulness.

description: Regional variation in the number of cancer centers creates the need for specific regional coordination for data collection, adding logistical complexity for the research team.
justification: This operational constraint hampers designers' ability to understand context of use and to facilitate consistent participant recruitment and data collection across sites, which can impede evaluation and iteration workloads.
reference_excerpt: The number of cancers centers varies by region, requiring specific regional coordination for data collection.

description: The bending (flex) sensors used on the leaf springs could not provide accurate absolute angle measurements and could only resolve large angle deviations (~20°), limiting precise motion sensing.
justification: Limited sensor fidelity constrained the team's ability to accurately measure fine finger joint rotations and therefore impeded understanding of real movement context and reliable evaluation of gesture-based interactions during design iterations.
reference_excerpt: The integrated bending sensors in the leaf springs at the ﬁngers are good enough to differentiate between different grasps,36 and can detect small changes of motion, but are only able to resolve between large absolute angle deviations of roughly 20 degrees.37 These limitation are caused not by the mechanism itself, but by the type of bending sensor used: the ﬂexible resistance-based sensors suffer from natural decay in step response that makes it hard to get accurate absolute values from the sensors.

description: The passive-actuated orthosis design could not automatically regulate physical assistance, so the system could not implement true 'assist-as-needed' adaptive support.
justification: This hardware constraint forced designers to adopt a software workaround (modulating game speed) rather than implement automatic assistance, limiting their ability to realize therapeutic interaction requirements and to prototype the intended adaptive assistance functionality.
reference_excerpt: However, the passive device does not allow any automatic regulation of the physical support provided, which is set by the therapist. Hence, the THRI further modulates the task difﬁculty using the speed of the game to prolong interaction time.

description: High inter-individual variability in motor symptoms among stroke survivors made gesture recognition and calibration challenging.
justification: User heterogeneity constrained the researchers' ability to generalise gesture recognition models and complicated calibration and evaluation workflows, hindering management of user understanding and reliable evaluation across diverse users.
reference_excerpt: One of the major challenges in performing gesture recognition with stroke survivors is the inter-individual variability in motor symptoms. For instance, while normative data about range of motion (ROM) for the upper limb joints is available for healthy subjects,39,40 each patient constitutes a per se case.

description: The calibration procedure did not succeed in all attempts (only ~85–88% success), and calibration durations varied substantially across movements.
justification: Incomplete and time-varying calibration reduced the reliability of gesture detection and therefore limited formative and summative evaluation activities as well as iterative refinement of the THRI and UI based on consistent measurement.
reference_excerpt: In a preliminary analysis of the data from seven subjects, we showed that such a procedure was effective in 85% of the attempts (1044 out of 1229 tests) with durations differing across movements of up to 30 s for hand opening.42 ... In total, the calibration procedure has been successful in 88% of the attempts (3791 out of 4298).

description: Participant dropouts occurred because users were unable to work with the system due to technical problems or loss of desire to continue.
justification: These dropouts directly impeded the researchers' ability to conduct summative evaluation and gather sufficient user data, constraining evaluation workloads and user involvement activities.
reference_excerpt: Among the ﬁrst 12 patients were two dropouts, because of their inability to work with the SCRIPT system due to technical problems, or no desire to work with the SCRIPT system anymore.

description: Ethical and safety constraints prevented direct testing in real emergency conditions, forcing reliance on theoretical, expert-advice, and controlled simulations.
justification: These constraints limited the team's ability to study real user behaviour under stress, conduct realistic evaluations, and thus manage evolving user understanding and evaluate designs in true contexts of use.
reference_excerpt: However, when considering the design process for a fire extinguisher, the ethical tenet of safety of research participants had to be at the forefront of the chosen methodology. Therefore, the adopted research methods listed next emphasize theoretical research, advice from professionals, and controlled environments during practical research. In conclusion, this project highlights the importance of a user-centered design process when designing equipment to be used in emergency situations, even though the ethics surrounding fire and fire studies make it difficult to do direct testing and research activities.

description: The work remained at concept stage without a functioning prototype, preventing rigorous testing, usability trials, and empirical validation of performance parameters.
justification: Lack of a physical prototype constrained the designers' ability to evaluate designs with users, iterate based on observed usability issues, and specify validated requirements (e.g., weight and activation force) for the target demographics.
reference_excerpt: The next stage in the design process would be to produce a functioning prototype, which would enable further testing and evaluation to confirm that the design is a viable improvement. As the proposed design reached only the concept stage, weight was not calculated, but the initial product evaluation conducted for the redesign indicated a total weight of 2 kg (when full).

description: Observed maintenance processes and records existed for public buildings but not for private residential dwellings, limiting empirical insight into home-maintenance behaviours.
justification: This contextual/data gap hindered the designers' ability to fully understand the private use and maintenance context of extinguishers, affecting the 'understand context of use' workload and the specification of realistic maintenance-related requirements.
reference_excerpt: The maintenance checks were thorough, and the records for extinguishers in public environments were extensive. No comparable process exists in private residential dwellings.

description: The project lacked budget to procure devices, forcing the team to rely only on existing user devices during design and testing.
justification: This financial constraint limited the team's ability to specify device requirements, produce and evaluate prototypes across consistent hardware, and plan realistic deployment scenarios.
reference_excerpt: It should be noted this project did not include funds for pro- curement of devices so only existing devices could be used.

description: Poor network connectivity and sporadic electricity in the field constrained what digital functionality could be designed and tested.
justification: Unreliable connectivity and power impeded the team's ability to evaluate digital designs in realistic conditions and required them to change design requirements (e.g., include paper-based tools), limiting iterative digital testing.
reference_excerpt: Network connectivity was poor, and electricity to charge phones was sporadic.

description: County governments lacked budgetary capacity to maintain separate software, forcing designers to constrain solutions to be sustainable without county-funded maintenance.
justification: This external funding and capacity limitation constrained specification of system requirements and design options (e.g., must work on personal phones, include paper backups), thus narrowing feasible prototypes and evaluation scenarios.
reference_excerpt: For the system to be sustainable, it had to be applicable for all CHVs across Kenya; these counties alone do not have the capacity or budget to maintain the software. CHVs would need to use personal phones as procuring devices was not possible; county budgets are limited and maintaining broken or lost devices over the long term was not feasible.

description: HCD requires specialized expertise that individuals working in government settings may not possess, making internal adoption and local leadership of the process difficult.
justification: Limited HCD knowledge among government stakeholders hindered the designers' ability to transfer methods, build local capacity, and coordinate multidisciplinary teams for sustained HCD activities and iterative implementation.
reference_excerpt: It should be noted that HCD requires specialized expertise to lead the process, and individuals working in governments of low- and middle-income coun- tries may not have these skills. At this time, HCD is a specialized methodology that requires external as- sistance.

description: The HCD process required substantial up-front time and resources (7 months), which exceeded typical timelines for program design.
justification: The long lead time constrained rapid iteration and increased resource demands on the design team, affecting their ability to integrate feedback quickly and potentially delaying evaluation and implementation activities.
reference_excerpt: Compared to other pro- gram design approaches, HCD and systems analysis can take a greater time investment up front (in this case it took 7 months). The approach requires significant time before implementation to conduct the research (2 to 3 months), thoroughly under- stand the end users (and establish trust with them), and develop and repeatedly test the design and high-fidelity prototypes of the solutions (2 to 3 months).

description: The development generated a large volume of qualitative data over a long timeline, imposing heavy analytic and incorporation work on developers.
justification: Processing, analyzing and incorporating >100 hours of interview material over two years directly increased workload and slowed the team's ability to integrate feedback and iterate prototypes, hindering manage user understanding and integrate feedback & iteration workloads.
reference_excerpt: The development process spanned over two years and involved 58 participants, resulting in > 100 h of interview material and feedback that needed to be processed, analyzed and incorporated in successive rounds.

description: Diverse and conflicting preferences among stakeholders and users made it difficult to reconcile views and reach consensus on design decisions.
justification: Conflicting feedback (e.g., some users preferring closed navigation while others found it restrictive) impeded the team's ability to specify user requirements and integrate feedback across rounds, limiting iteration and evaluation decisions.
reference_excerpt: Additionally, engaging many different users provides a variety of perspectives, but can pose a larger challenge to integrate these diverse views and find a consensus, particularly in the area of usability testing. For instance, some participants found the PDA’s closed navigation essential to guide the user through the process while others felt it was too restrictive.

description: There was limited guidance on how to adapt decision aids for elderly users, leaving designers without clear evidence-based methods for this target group.
justification: A lack of established guidance on designing for older audiences constrained the team's ability to fully understand the context of use and specify appropriate requirements for usability and accessibility for elderly patients.
reference_excerpt: Moreover, there is little guidance on how to adapt PDAs for an older audience, leading the reviewers to emphasize the importance of proper design and testing. Visual support in the form of diagrams and animations is considered particularly beneficial.

description: No established governance or maintenance structure existed to keep the PDA technologically and scientifically up-to-date, requiring ongoing collaboration that was not yet organized.
justification: The absence of a governance structure and agreed maintenance responsibilities limits the designers' ability to sustain iterative updates, coordinate multidisciplinary actors, and manage evolving user understanding over time.
reference_excerpt: It is important to ensure that a PDA stays up-to-date on current developments and new therapies, which requires developers and clinicians to collaborate continuously. Therefore, it may be valuable to establish a governance structure within the hospital for maintaining the PDA and collecting and analyzing data about its effectiveness to be shared with clinicians and the wider medical community to create awareness.

description: The COVID-19 pandemic and social-distancing measures prevented Centering Pregnancy (CP) group-care from taking place, blocking inclusion of CP in the large-scale trial.
justification: This external constraint directly hindered the designers' ability to evaluate the CP intervention in a planned large-scale trial, impeding the 'evaluate designs' workload and limiting real-world testing and iteration.
reference_excerpt: However, due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the associated social-distancing measured in place at the time of the data collection, CP group-care could not safely take place and could therefore not be included in the large-scale trial.

description: CP care was only offered in a limited number of clinics, preventing random assignment of midwifery clinics to CP or control conditions.
justification: This operational constraint limited the designers' ability to use the intended semi-randomized design for evaluation, constraining the 'evaluate designs' workload and robust testing of the CP intervention.
reference_excerpt: We planned to use a semi-randomized design because participating midwifery clinics could not be randomly assigned to the CP or control condition, as CP care is only offered in a limited number of clinics.

description: The development pre-tests used small sample sizes that were insufficient to evaluate effectiveness or support broad generalizability of findings.
justification: Small sample sizes constrained the designers' ability to generalize user insights and to robustly assess intervention outcomes, limiting the 'manage user understanding' and 'evaluate designs' workloads.
reference_excerpt: The small sample sizes in this study do not serve to evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention. They merely served to improve the intervention during the development process.

description: Midwives' personal attitudes toward vaccination vary and some who are critical may be less inclined to follow the training.
justification: Because midwives are key facilitators of CP, their attitudes and potential reluctance to adopt training can undermine implementation fidelity and the designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and coordinate multidisciplinary delivery.
reference_excerpt: Midwives play an important role as facilitators in the CP intervention. ... midwives who are critical of vaccination may be less inclined to follow the training.

description: Reaching at-risk populations (low health literacy and low SES) with online interventions is more challenging.
justification: This limitation impeded the designers' ability to ensure inclusive user involvement and manage understanding for all target subgroups, affecting 'manage user understanding' and 'facilitate user involvement' workloads and motivating the parallel development of a non-online CP intervention.
reference_excerpt: However, even though online interventions can be effective, the reach of at-risk populations (i.e., those with low (health) literacy and socio-economic status) is more challenging (23, 24).

description: Public health staff were extremely busy during the COVID-19 pandemic, forcing the team to abandon traditional, resource-intensive HCD methods and adopt pragmatic alternatives (e.g., reviewing existing dashboards, virtual meetings).
justification: Limited availability of stakeholder staff constrained the designers' ability to conduct contextual inquiry and extended domain workshops, hindering the workloads of managing user understanding, facilitating user involvement, and understanding context of use.
reference_excerpt: First, traditional human-centered design methods were modified to be more pragmatic, which was critical during the COVID-19 pandemic ... when public health staff were incredibly busy. The pragmatic modifications included learning from existing data dashboards instead of starting from scratch and conducting virtual meetings instead of observing user behavior in their workplace.

description: Sensitive data and confidential workspaces prevented the research team from gaining security clearances to observe users in their workplace.
justification: Restricted access to users' workplace interactions directly prevented contextual inquiry, reducing designers' ability to understand the real context of use and gather rich, in-situ user insights needed for specifying requirements and producing solutions.
reference_excerpt: Both were impractical in our context, between staff being diverted to the COVID-19 response (thereby severely constraining their time) and staff working in confidential spaces due to the sensitive data (thereby making it difficult for a researcher team to gain security clearances to observe workflows directly).

description: Conducting virtual meetings limited the types of observational data the team could collect (for example, eye movements and facial expressions).
justification: The loss of rich observational cues hindered the designers' ability to fully evaluate user interactions and read nonverbal signals during usability testing, constraining the evaluation and manage user understanding workloads and limiting fidelity of feedback for iteration.
reference_excerpt: Our virtual meetings in Steps 3 and 4 may have been limited compared to the traditional methods because the data collection was not in the users’ work environment, and we could not collect some potentially useful data such as eye movements or facial expressions.

description: Participant recruitment relied on practitioners already closely connected to the AIDS Institute who were knowledgeable about STIs but had limited prior experience with data dashboards, and evaluators/participants may not reflect all stakeholder opinions.
justification: This sampling approach limited the diversity and representativeness of user perspectives available to designers, constraining their ability to manage user understanding, specify requirements for different user types, and ensure designs meet needs of all stakeholder groups.
reference_excerpt: we recruited participants from practitioners who already had close relationships with the AIDS Institute as community-based public health champions... these participants were knowledgeable about STIs but most of them had little previous experience with data dashboards... although the evaluators and participants comprised diverse groups, their opinions may not reflect all stakeholders’ opinions.

description: State government 'executive clearance' requirements mandated that the final dashboard be hosted on an external organization's website and that each website update be reviewed before public release.
justification: This external governance and approval constraint limited designers' deployment options and could slow or complicate iterative releases and rapid integration of feedback, thereby hindering integrate feedback & iteration and coordination with stakeholders.
reference_excerpt: Another finding was that the final data dashboard would need to be hosted on an external organization’s website due to state government agency “executive clearance” requirements that each website update be reviewed and approved before release to the public.

description: Behavioral and computer science team members had gaps in shared domain knowledge and assumptions, leaving important navigation rules and edge cases unspecified.
justification: This lack of shared technical and domain knowledge hindered coordination of the multidisciplinary team and prevented complete specification of user requirements, forcing later rework and limiting efficient iteration and integration of feedback.
reference_excerpt: potentially important navigation rules were left unspecified (ie, use of the web browser’s back button, entry of spaces, or nonlanguage text as open-ended responses). These and similar oversights may be owing to behavioral scientists’ implicit assumptions and lack of familiarity with the problems that such errors can cause, and thus, failing to specify all desired rules ahead of time.

description: Key technical specification steps were skipped during the build (eg, tagging peer profiles with age indicators and preventing nonlanguage responses), and were postponed as substantial revisions.
justification: Omitting these specification details directly impeded the team's ability to produce correct design solutions and to fully evaluate the prototype with intended data structures, delaying iteration and subsequent user testing.
reference_excerpt: The application specifications did not include procedures for preventing nonlanguage text responses to the open-ended questions. In contrast, the peer profiles were intended to be tagged with age indicators (similar to peer images), but this step was skipped in the build process... As the latter two issues were deemed substantial revisions, they were noted and postponed until a future round of substantive updates.

description: Lengthy and complex IRB and institutional permission processes (including server-hosting permissions) delayed development and testing.
justification: Regulatory and institutional constraints consumed time and required additional communication, which hindered the team's ability to iterate quickly, schedule testing, and maintain momentum for user-centered activities.
reference_excerpt: we encountered difficulties regarding questions about permissions for server housing and IRB questions about the collection of protected health information via the new web application. The process of effectively communicating this to the IRB and securing permission to house the web application on a commercial server was lengthy and involved. This was one of the several delays in the large process of web application development and testing that contributed to the extension of the project time line.

description: Limited financial and personnel resources for formative-stage work constrained activities such as recording interviews, multiple raters, and more robust evaluation procedures.
justification: Resource scarcity prevented the team from implementing stronger evaluation practices and from protecting team members' time, thereby limiting the rigor of data collection, the ability to triangulate findings, and the quality of user understanding.
reference_excerpt: In future studies, it would be ideal to record interviews and have multiple raters use a standard set of guidelines. However, it is important to note that these procedures may not be possible at formative study stages owing to limited financial support to protect team members’ time for such activities. Relative to the resources available for later stages of the process... research funding for the formative stages of tool development is often much more modest.

description: All participant interviews and feedback sessions were conducted by the principal investigator, raising risks of social desirability and confirmation bias.
justification: Centralizing data collection in one investigator—driven by available resources and staffing choices—limited the team's ability to manage user understanding objectively and reduced methodological rigor during evaluation.
reference_excerpt: All data collection processes and feedback sessions with women in midlife were conducted by the first author (DA), who is the principal investigator of the project. Knowing that they were speaking to the project director may have heightened the participants’ social desirability or self-presentation behaviors. The first author’s direct involvement can also enable confirmation bias regarding the conclusions drawn.

description: The COVID-19 pandemic redirected investigator time and priorities, causing additional delays in development and testing.
justification: This external disruption reduced available staff time and slowed iteration and coordination, constraining the team's ability to conduct planned user-centered activities and maintain the development timeline.
reference_excerpt: The onset of the COVID-19 pandemic was the cause of another delay, as part of the investigators’ research time was redirected to other professional and personal responsibilities.

description: Designers faced resource constraints (funding, space, coordination) that limit the feasibility of implementing prototypes at scale.
justification: Lack of funding, physical spaces and coordination capacity prevents designers from refining, scaling and evaluating prototypes in real service settings, hindering production of design solutions and iterative testing.
reference_excerpt: Issues like manicure funding, the provision of physical spaces in waiting rooms, and the coordination of waiting times with medical care should be reviewed.

description: Healthcare centers lacked capacity to absorb demand induced by the 'Encanto' prototype, constraining designers' ability to test real-world uptake.
justification: If health centers cannot schedule Pap test appointments in a timely manner, designers cannot validly evaluate uptake or iteratively improve the experience based on real attendance data, hindering evaluation and facilitation of user involvement.
reference_excerpt: Finally, due to the appeal of the service, the healthcare center must attend to the demand induced by ‘Encanto’ and schedule Pap test appointments in a timely manner.

description: Older women had difficulty handling touchscreen tablets, reducing designers' ability to include them in usability testing and interactional evaluation.
justification: Low digital literacy among some participants prevented effective interaction with the app prototype, hindering designers' ability to evaluate designs, understand context of use, and facilitate inclusive user involvement.
reference_excerpt: The tablet was not an adequate tool for women over 60 years old, who had difficulty handling a touchscreen.

description: Beacon-delivered messages produced notifications but resulted in few users effectively accessing the linked video, limiting outreach effectiveness.
justification: Low effective access to the video via Beacons prevented designers from reaching and testing with target users in their contexts, constraining evaluation of the media-based prototype and its iterations.
reference_excerpt: After analyzing the data, it was determined that, although there were 297 message notifications in the targeted cellphones, few people had effective access to the video.

description: The project lacked a follow-up mechanism and interoperable information systems to link outreach messages to clinic visits, limiting outcome evaluation.
justification: Without systems to identify which women were reached and whether they subsequently attended clinics, designers cannot measure effectiveness or integrate feedback for the media strategy, hindering evaluation and management of user understanding.
reference_excerpt: in order to value the effectiveness of the media-based strategy, a follow-up mechanism must be included that can identify the women outreached with this technology and, subsequently those who visited primary healthcare centers to take a Pap test.

description: The Citobot required further hardware modifications and additional clinical and AI development before it could match existing devices and be validated.
justification: Technical limitations (narrower viewing angle) and the need for AI algorithm development and clinical validation prevented designers from finalizing the device and fully evaluating its performance in context, hindering production of robust design solutions and evaluation.
reference_excerpt: However, the speculum’s viewing angle was greater than that of the Citobot, so this device requires further modifications in hardware development. ... In subsequent studies, we will advance clinical research to determine the acceptability, reproducibility, sensitivity, and specificity, concordance with cytology, and predictive capacity of the Citobot. At the same time, we will develop the machine learning algorithms of the AI incorporated into this medical device.

description: There were no suitable off-the-shelf measurement interfaces, and budget and time constraints forced the team to develop an early prototype in-house.
justification: Lack of available hardware and limited funding/time constrained the team's ability to procure existing tools, increasing workload for producing design solutions and slowing iteration and evaluation activities.
reference_excerpt: Design of an early prototype for palpation training was planned due to a lack of available oﬀ-the-shelf measurement interfaces with the ﬂexibility required for this study. Moreover, additional factors such as budget restrictions and time commitments were inﬂuential in making this decision.

description: End users were not available for early evaluation, so proxies (colleagues) were used instead to run Cognitive Walkthroughs.
justification: Unavailability of real end-users limited authentic user involvement and evaluation, reducing the team's ability to manage evolving user understanding and to integrate user feedback effectively in early iterations.
reference_excerpt: Cognitive Walkthrough was used to evaluate the early prototype, when an end-user is not available with the help of proxies (e.g. fellow colleagues) to ensure it complies with the domain principles which were extracted via literature reviews and process observations.

description: Ethnographic field methods were considered infeasible because they are costly and time-consuming, preventing long-term embedded observations.
justification: The inability to perform extended ethnographic studies limited the team's capacity to deeply understand real training contexts and constrained the 'understand context of use' and 'manage user understanding' workloads.
reference_excerpt: ethnography (or ﬁeld study) is one of the most eﬀective methods in ergonomics studies to determine challenges and collect information about conventional practice. However, it is a costly and time consuming method in which the investigator is physically involved/embedded in the whole training programme (in medical school) for long-term investigations.

description: Only four senior clinical tutors were involved in developing the ground-truth model, and the authors state more expert collaboration was required.
justification: Limited expert participation constrained the team's ability to produce a robust, generalisable best-practice model and hindered specifying reliable user requirements and validating assessment criteria.
reference_excerpt: Four senior clinical tutors were involved in order to develop a ground theory in a limited timeframe and more collaboration from experts are required to improve eﬃciency and reliability of the proposed approach.

description: Recruitment difficulties and participant withdrawals reduced representation across body types and genders (e.g., no large female volunteers; a male withdrew prior to data collection).
justification: Restricted access to diverse actor patients limited the team's ability to understand context-of-use variability and to create an averaged anatomy model, hindering evaluation and generalisability of findings.
reference_excerpt: It was diﬃcult to ﬁnd a female participant in the Large category as no one within that category volunteered and it was deemed unethical to ask individuals directly. Just prior to the start of the data collection, the male participant in the medium body category withdrew.

description: Institutional permissions limited changes to room layout, restricting where the TFT display could be placed during experiments.
justification: Restricted room/setting permissions prevented designing ideal real-world evaluation setups and constrained evaluation and user involvement practices (e.g., positioning feedback displays close to patients), reducing ecological validity of tests.
reference_excerpt: The investigator had limited permissions to change the room settings to position the TFT display next to the patient’s face.

description: Current sensing and multimodal visualisation technologies are not yet sufficiently advanced or robust, requiring further research to achieve reliable quantification.
justification: Technical limitations of sensors and displays constrained the fidelity of prototypes and the team's ability to produce high‑fidelity solutions and fully evaluate them, impacting iteration and implementation planning.
reference_excerpt: Measuring the human ergonomics demands advancement in sensory technologies and multimodal visualisation displays. Thus, more research is needed in this domain to guide future researchers and developers towards robust and reliable quantiﬁcation techniques.

description: Physical design issues were reported by participants (glove size for small hands, left‑handedness, and exposure of electronics to patient skin), indicating the prototype did not fully meet diverse user requirements.
justification: These usability and safety concerns limited the team's ability to satisfy user requirements and produce an unintrusive, inclusive design, thereby constraining further iteration and wider user testing.
reference_excerpt: In particular, the following concerns raised among the answers; Paying attention to the patient’s face during familiarisation stage, glove size for small hands and left handedness, exposure of the electronics to patient’s skin.

description: The research team did not record reasons for non-participation or characteristics of non-participants, leaving gaps in understanding who was excluded from study phases.
justification: Lack of data on non-participants limited the designers' ability to manage user understanding and to ensure representative recruitment for HCD activities (understand context of use and facilitate user involvement).
reference_excerpt: Reasons for non-participation and characteristics of the non-participant cohort were not recorded.

description: The community advisory board (CAB) comprised only eight members, so community input beyond those directly associated with the study came from a relatively small number of individuals.
justification: Limited stakeholder representation constrained the designers' ability to manage evolving community understanding and to facilitate broader user involvement during planning and feedback phases.
reference_excerpt: Additionally, our community advisory board included only eight members, so our community input beyond those directly associated with the study came from a relatively small number of individuals.

description: The study focused recruitment on variation in print literacy and excluded patients with cognitive disabilities or poor English proficiency, potentially missing important perspectives.
justification: Excluding these groups reduced the designers' ability to fully understand the range of user needs and contexts of use, limiting requirement specification and inclusive design decisions.
reference_excerpt: For example, patients with cognitive disabilities or with poor English proficiency may have perspectives that differ from the broader low print literacy population.  ...  we chose to focus our recruitment strategy on ensuring variation in print literacy levels.

description: Patients did not participate directly in the ideation workshop; designers relied on patient quotes and suggestions instead of real-time co-creation.
justification: Absence of direct patient participation limited facilitation of user involvement and constrained real-time integration of user feedback during ideation, affecting iteration and solution generation.
reference_excerpt: Although patients did not participate in the ideation workshop, we engaged co-creation and participatory processes [58, 59] by incorporating direct patient quotes and patient suggestions into the discussion.

description: The original interface was created by an experienced programming team that lacked usability training, producing design decisions not grounded in usability practice.
justification: Designers' lack of usability knowledge hindered their ability to produce user-centered design solutions and required the HCD team to expend effort correcting foundational interface choices, affecting specification of requirements and iterative design work.
reference_excerpt: This interface was designed by a skilled, experienced programming team, though untrained in usability.

description: Heterogeneous user perspectives and split questionnaire ratings produced ambiguous feedback that demanded additional analysis to interpret.
justification: Ambiguous and split user feedback increased the analytic burden on designers, impeding timely integration of feedback and iteration and complicating the specification of clear user requirements and priorities.
reference_excerpt: each from different agencies with somewhat differing user cultures; e.g., some involved the use of more students than others. Split ratings often indicate problem areas, but require more analysis of user comments than more consistent ratings.

description: Limitations of the incumbent and planned EHRs prevented building the mobile, paperless workflow inside the EHR and forced the team to develop an external, interoperable application.
justification: EHR platform constraints limited the designers' ability to produce and iterate design solutions within the primary clinical system, hindering rapid development, integration, and evaluation workflows.
reference_excerpt: Our decision to build the application alongside (rather than within) the main EHR was largely motivated by our requirement of supporting a mobile, paperless handoff and rounding workflow. This was not possible within our EHR at the time (Allscripts) nor within the EHR our health system planned to implement shortly thereafter (Epic). Moreover, our team needed a platform that enabled rapid development with frequent iterations, which is often not feasible in a large, foundational application such as the EHR of a large health system.

description: An external electronic survey used during pilot phases was poorly utilized and created challenges for the development team to respond in a timely manner.
justification: Poor uptake of the initial feedback channel hindered the designers' ability to manage user understanding and integrate feedback and iteration rapidly, prompting a change in feedback mechanisms.
reference_excerpt: During pilot phases, application feedback was provided via an external electronic survey. This was poorly utilized and posed challenges to timely responses for our development team.

description: Limited availability of mobile devices, battery depletion, and uneven Wi‑Fi/cellular coverage in nonclinical areas constrained real-world mobile use.
justification: Infrastructure and device resource limitations restricted designers' ability to study and support the intended mobile context of use and to evaluate designs under realistic conditions.
reference_excerpt: We did encounter challenges to implementing our application, including availability of mobile devices for users and mobile device battery depletion. While Wi-Fi and cellular network coverage within clinical areas was adequate, the use of Carelign on mobile devices while en route to see patients revealed uneven coverage in nonclinical areas (e.g., hallways, staircases, and elevators).

description: Replacing paper lists with a mobile tool led to workflow mismatches when clinicians needed to reference lists during concurrent phone calls, forcing workarounds and continued reliance on printouts for some services.
justification: This interactional/workflow constraint prevented designers from fully addressing the holistic experience and from achieving a complete transition to mobile workflows, limiting iterative refinement and adoption testing of pure mobile scenarios.
reference_excerpt: Replacing paper lists with a mobile tool in some cases led to a workflow mismatch when users needed to reference their lists on their mobile device during a simultaneous phone call. However, when relying only on a mobile device, this occasionally required a workaround such as using a landline or headphones for the phone call, or alternatively keeping a list printout as a backup reference.

description: The implementation team had only two to three part-time clinical members and two to four part-time developers, limiting staffing capacity for training, support, and ongoing development.
justification: Limited personnel resources constrained the designers' ability to facilitate user involvement, provide continuous support, and rapidly implement iterative improvements and evaluations.
reference_excerpt: The implementation team consisted of two to three part-time clinical members for training and support and two to four part-time developers for building new features, addressing bugs and issues, and technical support.

description: Errors and omissions in data collection led to missing usage metrics for specific date ranges, undermining complete measurement of adoption and usage.
justification: Data collection errors impeded the designers' and researchers' ability to evaluate designs and measure usage reliably, limiting evidence for iterative decision-making and assessment.
reference_excerpt: Note: Due to an error in data collection, login sessions for the following date range were omitted from panel (B): 11/19/2017–1/20/2018.

description: Inherent limitations of the EHR prevented some physician feedback from being implemented in the final CDS tools, constraining designers' ability to realize proposed changes.
justification: This technical/organizational constraint impeded the designers' ability to integrate feedback and iterate the prototypes and limited their capacity to produce final design solutions that matched user recommendations.
reference_excerpt: Additionally, inherent EHR limitations prevented some physician feedback from being implemented in the final CDS tools that were deployed in the EHR.

description: Interviews were limited to physicians, so designers lacked input from other clinician roles (nurse practitioners, physician assistants, residents) that may have differing workflows and needs.
justification: This sampling limitation reduced the designers' ability to manage user understanding and to specify user requirements across all relevant user groups and contexts of use.
reference_excerpt: A limitation of our study is that interviews were limited to physicians; the input of nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and residents in training may have relevance for clinical implementation of CDS tools in differing clinical workﬂows.

description: Usability testing with patients was conducted virtually due to COVID-19, which prevented observation of nonverbal cues during sessions.
justification: The inability to observe nonverbal behavior limited researchers' ability to fully manage user understanding and to evaluate users' interactions and emotional responses during testing, hindering evaluation and context-of-use studies.
reference_excerpt: Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, usability testing sessions were conducted using videoconferencing software (Zoom Video Communications Inc). Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, usability testing sessions conducted with patients were virtual and nonverbal cues could not be observed; however, screen sharing along with open-ended questions allowed us to obtain sufficient feedback which was often consistent across participants.

description: FH Family Share was not integrated with the electronic health record, limiting ease of access across remote or underserved communities with diverse EHR systems.
justification: Lack of EHR integration constrained designers' ability to study and support real-world contexts of use and to facilitate involvement of users in certain settings, thereby hindering understanding context of use and facilitating user involvement for deployment.
reference_excerpt: Additionally, FH Family Share was not integrated with the electronic health record to enable ease of access in remote or underserved communities which may have different electronic health record systems in place.

description: Usability testing was limited to genetic counselors and patients and did not include family members of patients.
justification: Excluding family members prevented designers from obtaining input from an important user group, limiting their ability to manage user understanding and to plan for implementation in nonclinical settings where family members are key actors.
reference_excerpt: Usability testing sessions were limited to genetic counselors and patients with familial hypercholesterolemia—input from family members of patients with familial hypercholesterolemia would be useful in ensuring effective implementation of the tool in nonclinical settings.

description: The study sample was small and not representative of the larger HSCT caregiver population, limiting the breadth of user data available to designers.
justification: Limited and non-representative sampling constrained designers' ability to manage user understanding and to specify user requirements that generalize across diverse caregiver contexts, reducing confidence in evaluation and iteration decisions.
reference_excerpt: First, although we collected data from three different transplant centers, our sample sizes are not representative of the larger HSCT caregiver population. Future work should include large, diverse samples of caregivers with varying levels of health literacy.

description: The study omitted HSCT recipients, so designers lacked the recipient perspective needed to understand dyadic interactions and dual needs.
justification: Not including recipients prevented designers from addressing the holistic caregiver–recipient experience and hindered their ability to fully understand context of use and to specify requirements that consider both parties.
reference_excerpt: Second, our study did not include HSCT recipients. A future direction of our work is to build knowledge of how HIT-enabled tools can dually benefit caregivers and HSCT recipients.

description: Transplant providers reported they have little insight into caregiver burden after discharge, limiting the observational and clinical data available to the design team.
justification: Providers' limited post-discharge contact constrained designers' ability to understand the real-world context of use and to manage evolving user understanding over the full care trajectory, impeding requirements specification and evaluation for post-discharge support.
reference_excerpt: All three transplant centers admit they have little insight about burden on caregivers after discharge, as much of the interaction with caregivers is pre- and during the HSCT.

description: There is a sparse evidence base of prior HIT interventions for HSCT caregivers, with nearly all existing interventions delivered in-person.
justification: A limited precedent of technology-enabled interventions reduced designers' available domain knowledge and examples to draw on when specifying user requirements, producing design solutions, and planning evaluations tailored to this population.
reference_excerpt: We found that few interventions for HSCT caregivers leverage HIT [10]. Our review indicated that nearly all caregiver interventions were delivered in-person. Only one study used a technology-enabled intervention.

description: Later-round testing required participants to have internet access at home to review the system, which constrained who could participate.
justification: Requiring home internet access limited participant recruitment and thus hindered designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and to understand the real-world context of use for the system.
reference_excerpt: As we moved to later rounds of user testing, it was also necessary for participants to have internet access at home to review the recording system before the usability session.

description: The participant sample was predominantly White and college educated, limiting designers' knowledge about diverse user needs.
justification: A non-diverse sample constrained the team's ability to manage user understanding and to specify user requirements for underrepresented groups, reducing confidence that design decisions met broader user needs.
reference_excerpt: Our sample was predominately White and college educated, reflecting the demographics of the region where our study took place. Further work is needed with individuals from more diverse ethnic and racial groups and from those with lower educational attainment levels.

description: Usability testing was conducted in controlled lab settings rather than in naturalistic environments.
justification: Testing in controlled settings prevented designers from fully understanding the real-world context of use and limited their ability to evaluate how the system would perform and be used in everyday settings.
reference_excerpt: Our project was conducted in controlled settings, where participants were asked to think aloud and received assistance, if needed, with tasks. Although this is important at this stage of user design, it does not reflect the user experience in naturalistic settings.

description: Task instructions were sometimes unclear (eg, participants opened external tabs), which inflated critical incidents and confounded usability measurement.
justification: Unclear task design and facilitation reduced the team's ability to reliably evaluate designs and to integrate valid feedback for iteration, hindering accurate assessment of usability.
reference_excerpt: Some participants may have been unclear on the task instructions related to finding additional information (opening tabs outside of the UI), which may have resulted in the higher reported critical incidents in round 5 relative to our other usability metrics, that is, high SUS scores and task completion rate.

description: Introduction of hyperlinks, filters, and advanced search caused user confusion—particularly among older adults unfamiliar with modern UI affordances—leading to critical incidents.
justification: Users' unfamiliarity with these UI elements hindered designers' ability to evaluate and iterate the features (integrate feedback & iteration and evaluate designs) because observed problems reflected user interpretation issues rather than clear design faults.
reference_excerpt: The greatest number of challenges was observed in round 4, where hyperlinks were added. This resulted in confusion in finding sections of audio recordings to play using tags and using associated hyperlinks to find further information. Although participants became comfortable with most features, some features such as hyperlinks, filters, and the advanced search caused some confusion in the final round of testing. These challenges may be explained by a lack of familiarity with the modern UI design...

description: All usability testing used a laptop-only interface, leaving mobile contexts untested.
justification: Limiting testing to laptops prevented designers from understanding mobile contexts of use and evaluating mobile-specific interactions, constraining the specification of user requirements and future iteration for mobile devices.
reference_excerpt: Finally, we used a laptop computer for all usability testing sessions, but we hope to create a mobile adaptive UI, which will require further testing.

description: Usability testing is conducted by the external vendor (Pivot Design Group) and data are shared with the research team only in aggregate, limiting researchers' direct access to raw user data. This restricts designers' ability to inspect detailed think-aloud outputs and participant-level findings.
justification: Aggregated reporting and external conduction of usability sessions hinder designers' ability to manage user understanding, evaluate designs deeply, and integrate granular feedback for iteration because they cannot access or analyze individual-level interaction data.
reference_excerpt: We will recruit usability participants from our network via email, and their participation will be consented by Pivot Design Group, who will conduct the testing. Data will be collected for development purposes only and shared with the research team in aggregate.

description: The study intentionally provides minimal direction about the nature of target EBIs because it is unknown for which types of innovations the tool will be useful, creating uncertainty about target use cases. This vagueness limits the specificity of user requirements and contextual constraints for design.
justification: Lack of clarity about the kinds of EBIs to support hinders designers' ability to understand context of use and to specify concrete user requirements, which in turn constrains the production of tailored design solutions and focused evaluation criteria.
reference_excerpt: We will intentionally provide minimal direction regarding the nature of the target EBIs since it is not yet known for what types of innovations it will be useful.

description: COVID-19 restrictions on gatherings prevented the team from running planned community events that would have facilitated participatory co-design and education activities.
justification: This limitation directly hindered the designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and iterate on interventions that relied on group engagement (e.g., the monthly storytelling event), reducing opportunities for feedback and co-creation.
reference_excerpt: Ultimately, we were not able to take this idea forward due to emerging COVID-19 restrictions limiting community gatherings at that time.

description: Withdrawal of humanitarian organizations and disrupted NGO pad distribution created an unstable supply chain for sanitary products within the settlement.
justification: This external supply disruption constrained designers' ability to evaluate and specify feasible, sustainable product solutions (e.g., LaunchPad business model) and to understand the context of use for menstrual products.
reference_excerpt: The supply chain of sanitary pads into the settlement has been severely disrupted with the withdrawal of humanitarian organizations due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

description: Securing construction materials and formal approval for land from government and humanitarian actors could take six months or longer, delaying larger-scale construction ideas.
justification: Lengthy approval and procurement processes by external stakeholders impeded designers' ability to produce and pilot larger infrastructure solutions (the Cocoon Maxi), affecting feasibility assessments and iteration timelines.
reference_excerpt: However, in speaking with community stakeholders, we learned that securing construction materials and approval for the land from the government and humanitarian actors could take six months or longer.

description: Heavy rains and poor road quality delayed material delivery and construction work during the pilot.
justification: Environmental and logistical constraints slowed implementation and prototyping timelines, directly impeding designers' ability to produce design solutions and iterate within the planned schedule.
reference_excerpt: Heavy rains in the settlement delayed work, as the settlement’s roads are of poor quality, and vehicles run the risk of getting stuck when they flood. This led to a delay in material delivery.

description: Logistical and financial challenges prevented installing an incinerator at every Mini site despite user preference for on-site disposal.
justification: Resource and cost constraints limited designers' ability to address a critical user requirement (at-source disposal), thereby constraining the holistic experience and preventing full alignment of the solution with user needs.
reference_excerpt: Many participants requested an incinerator be attached to each Mini, though this posed logistical and financial challenges. Two incinerators were therefore constructed alongside one Mini structure in either village to reduce travel time to existing incinerators.

description: Limited time and resources produced a short three-month pilot and constrained sample size and sampling methods.
justification: Time and resource shortages hindered designers' ability to conduct longer-term evaluation and to gather representative data, restricting the evaluation workload and the capacity to assess sustained use and long-term outcomes.
reference_excerpt: The Mini users recruited for this study were chosen from a convenience sample, and the sample size was limited by available resources and time constraints. ...pilot data collection was conducted only over a short three-month period...

description: Familiarity between Kuja Kuja interviewers (community members) and participants may have introduced social desirability bias into data collection.
justification: This interactional trust/familiarity risked biasing responses and thus hindered the designers' ability to reliably manage user understanding and synthesize accurate insights for design decisions.
reference_excerpt: Kuja Kuja staff, who are members of the Bidi Bidi community, recruited participants, conducted interviews, and transcribed answers into English. Though the familiarity between interviewers and participants likely provided a more comfortable atmosphere for interviews, we recognize that it may have also introduced social desirability bias into the study.

description: Many Mini users lacked basic menstrual health supplies, but providing these supplies was out of the financial scope of the study, limiting full functionality of the intervention.
justification: Financial constraints prevented designers from supplying soap, buckets, and pads that users requested, limiting the designers' ability to deliver a holistic solution and to evaluate real-world usability and uptake under fully supported conditions.
reference_excerpt: While providing MH supplies was out of the financial scope of this study, future projects may benefit from including these commodities.

description: The settlement's existing infrastructure means findings may not generalize to more emergent humanitarian settings, limiting external applicability.
justification: This contextual limitation constrained designers' ability to specify user requirements and plan scalable adaptations for different contexts, affecting future design and implementation work.
reference_excerpt: Finally, the Bidi Bidi Settlement is well-established and has some pre-existing infrastructure; therefore, our study findings and implementation strategy may not be generalizable to other humanitarian settings that are more emergent.

description: Some co-design ideas required ongoing compensation and sensitization (e.g., for parents and husbands) to secure community participation, representing recurring resource needs.
justification: The team's recognition that events would need continuous investment limited their ability to implement certain participatory activities, constraining facilitation of user involvement and long-term engagement.
reference_excerpt: Furthermore, such an event would require an ongoing investment in both compensation for attendance and sensitization efforts with parents and husbands of participants to garner full community support.

description: Insufficient water access and drying spaces in the settlement undermined the viability of reusable-pad interventions.
justification: Operational context limitations (lack of water/drying) prevented designers from advancing the LaunchPad prototype to pilot, constraining production of a sustainable solution and evaluation of that concept.
reference_excerpt: Girls were concerned about maintaining their reusable pads without regular access to water and spaces for drying. Furthermore, because of fluctuations in pad distribution by NGOs, the supply and demand of pads remain inconsistent in the settlement, which could compromise the business model of uninterrupted sales.

description: Budget and time constraints forced the team to prioritize a minimal set of interactive features and leave additional features as static backlog illustrations.
justification: This resource constraint limited the designers' ability to produce full interactive design solutions and to iterate on and integrate additional feature concepts into the working prototype.
reference_excerpt: Given our budget and time constraints, we prioritized a set of minimal features for our interactive timeline prototype and rendered the backlog content as supplemental static illustrations of additional feature designs.

description: The evaluation was limited by remote, unsupervised testing with a small number of participants and weak statistical power.
justification: These limitations constrained the team's ability to robustly evaluate the prototype with users, reducing confidence in testing results and hindering effective integration of feedback and iteration based on representative user data.
reference_excerpt: There are limitations to this design project. Evaluation of this timeline was completed using expert reviews from a group of clinicians (physicians, nurses, pharmacists), human factors researchers, usability practitioners, and volunteers from the EHR vendor community. Our pilot study was performed unsupervised, remotely, and had a small number of participants with weak statistical power.

description: Inconsistent and limited prescription, dispense, and adherence data exchange across EHR and pharmacy systems, plus transformations into unstructured text, impeded creation of a precise timeline display.
justification: These external data and interoperability problems prevented designers from reliably understanding the real data context of use and from specifying and producing accurate timeline representations and evaluating them with authentic data.
reference_excerpt: We learned from implementation efforts at 1 EHR vendor and 1 client organization that there is inconsistent and limited prescription dispense and adherence data being exchanged or available currently. The transmission of e-prescription details is inconsistent across commercial EHR and pharmacy software products, thus limiting the consistent display of prescription instruction detail. When the data are exchanged from EHR to e-prescribing hub to pharmacy software, or make the return trip for a renewal request, the data may undergo transformation that introduces new ambiguity.

description: Target users were unfamiliar with the novel concept of content-based visual search, making it hard for designers to introduce and validate the approach with users.
justification: Users' inability to readily adopt the content-based search concept hindered the designers' work to manage user understanding and to facilitate meaningful user involvement and feedback during early requirement elicitation.
reference_excerpt: We learned that for all users the general idea was inspiring. Still, it was difficult for them to adapt the concept of searching in the data content, since this possibility was not given before.

description: A 'chicken-and-egg' dilemma existed: developers needed well-defined user requirements to build prototypes, while users needed prototypes or visual inspiration to articulate requirements.
justification: This mutual dependency explicitly impeded the designers' ability to specify user requirements and plan effective iterative prototyping cycles, constraining the process of producing and validating design solutions.
reference_excerpt: Be aware of this classical “chicken-and-egg” dilemma originating from knowledge gaps between different stakeholders [52]: on one hand, it is difficult for the computer scientist to provide a prototype without well-defined user requirements derived from domain knowledge. On the other hand, users will have difficulties in defining requirements without any visual inspiration derived from expertise in visualization designs.

description: Scientists expressed limited trust in third-party data and questioned the precision of overview visualizations, preferring data from trusted colleagues.
justification: This trust and precision concern limited designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and to address the holistic user experience, forcing them to invest additional effort into data curation and tightly integrated detail-on-demand to gain users' acceptance.
reference_excerpt: Many scientists prefer to analyze primarily their own data, or data they receive from colleague scientists they trust. Moreover, using advanced visualization capability was seen in a bipolar way by some scientists. On the one hand, it was recognized that visual overviews can greatly enhance screening and comparison tasks. On the other hand, scientists were questioning the precision of the visual representations of the data.

description: Users had varied and uncertain notions of time-series similarity, wanting many alternative similarity definitions, while designers feared overloading the system with too many parameters.
justification: This tension constrained the designers' ability to specify stable user requirements and to produce design solutions that balance flexibility and usability, complicating the definition of actionable similarity options and iteration strategies.
reference_excerpt: Still, we learned that scientists are often not entirely sure about how to formally define the perspective similarity for their search. As scientists pointed out, they ideally want to have many different similarity definitions at hand, and compare the search results they obtain, to decide upon the most appropriate similarity function. Yet our assumption is that overloading the search system with too many parameters (e.g., similarity search parameters) would detriment the usability and make the learning process more complicated.

description: Early stages of the project lacked a sufficiently integrative focus on usability, and the team recognized that earlier usability assessment would have been desirable.
justification: The absence of early, embedded usability attention hindered the designers' ability to manage user familiarization, to integrate feedback early, and to iteratively evaluate prototypes efficiently, increasing learning costs for users and rework for designers.
reference_excerpt: One of the lessons learned is that the usability of the system needs to be well grounded. Looking back, an even more integrative approach, especially in the early design stages, would have been desirable. A lesson learned for future projects is to make early assessment of usability aspects mandatory.

description: Early prototype interaction and interface design features (e.g., Visual Catalog colormap, loading cell patterns into the Sketch Editor, sketching interaction, and facet design) were confusing to users and impeded task completion.
justification: These concrete usability failings constrained designers' ability to evaluate and iterate effectively because participants struggled to perform core tasks, reducing the quality of feedback and necessitating substantial redesign work to support evaluation and iteration workloads.
reference_excerpt: Task 1 uncovered problems regarding the interface of the Visual Catalog. The applied colormap concept caused confusion since it was an unknown term for 10 participants (53%). Therefore, the colormap was removed in the following implementation phase. In task 2, most severities dealt with the problem that users were unsure how to use a cell pattern of the Visual Catalog as an example query and how it could be loaded into the Sketch Editor. With this version of the Sketch Editor, the users were unsure how to draw a curve pattern. Task 4 revealed that the concept of faceting was new to many users. It became clear that the facet design was not intuitive.

description: Legal COVID-19 restrictions forced focus groups to be conducted online, constraining in-person user engagement.
justification: Holding focus groups online limited designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and to study user context in person, hindering management of user understanding and requirement specification.
reference_excerpt: At that time, legal restrictions due to the COVID-19 pandemic prohibited on-site meetings. Thus, all focus groups were performed online.

description: A target user group (lung cancer support group) could not attend on-site usability sessions, reducing the number of participating groups.
justification: The absence of this group reduced participant diversity and limited the designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and collect representative usability data across contexts of use.
reference_excerpt: Since the app was provided on a test device for the second stage of usability testing, on-site meetings were necessary. As the lung cancer support group could not participate in meetings on-site, the number of participating groups reduced.

description: Participants without a private mobile device could not take part because the study could not provide smartphones.
justification: Excluding those without devices constrained recruitment and limited designers' ability to evaluate the app across the full user population and contexts of use.
reference_excerpt: As the app needed to be installed on a private mobile device, participants without a mobile device could not take part, as no one in the study could be provided with a smartphone.

description: The study failed to reach the planned ≥15 users for usability test 2, despite exceeding smaller critical thresholds.
justification: Insufficient participant numbers reduced statistical power and limited designers' ability to robustly evaluate and iterate on designs, hindering evaluation and integration of feedback.
reference_excerpt: Although the critical number of 5 persons was exceeded, the overall target of ≥15 users per usability test was not reached.

description: A coding error in the randomization prevented balanced assignment to app versions, producing uneven group sizes.
justification: This implementation error directly prevented planned group comparisons and therefore constrained the designers' ability to evaluate the effect of add-on features, hindering evaluation and iteration workloads.
reference_excerpt: Due to an error in the code, the randomized assignment of participants into the 3 versions (A, B, and C) did not lead to the same group size. Due to the uneven distribution of participants in the 3 app versions, group comparisons could not be performed.

description: A low number of male participants prevented sex-stratified analyses in some tests.
justification: Imbalanced gender participation limited designers' ability to analyze subgroup differences and to understand varied user experiences, hindering evaluation and requirement specification for different user groups.
reference_excerpt: Since the number of male participants was below the critical sum of 5 users, no further analysis stratified by sex was performed.

description: Older participants submitted fewer questionnaire responses, reducing data completeness for that subgroup.
justification: Age-related lower response rates constrained designers' ability to evaluate engagement and to understand usage patterns across ages, hindering management of user understanding and evaluation workloads.
reference_excerpt: Thus, the higher the age of the participant, the fewer the questionnaire responses submitted.

description: The choice of an online website platform was decided before the study began, constraining exploration of alternative platforms or delivery modes.
justification: Pre-specifying the platform limited designers' ability to investigate different formats or channels with users, hindering their work to manage user understanding, specify user requirements, and produce potentially more appropriate design solutions.
reference_excerpt: Another potential limitation of the study from a human centered or user centered design perspective is the type of online platform to meet users’ needs (a website) was already specified prior to the study commencing.

description: User research and usability testing lacked representation from key groups (LGBTIQA+, culturally and linguistically diverse people, and male partners).
justification: Insufficient representation constrained the designers' ability to develop a comprehensive, evolving understanding of diverse user needs and to facilitate involvement and iteration for those groups, limiting specification of inclusive requirements and evaluation validity.
reference_excerpt: One of the major limitations of the study was the lack of user research around the needs of those with limited representation including LGBTIQA+ people and those with broader culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds.

description: Eligibility criteria required good English and access to a computer with Zoom, excluding those without such access or literacy.
justification: These recruitment constraints prevented designers from involving and understanding users without English proficiency or internet/computer access, limiting the scope of user research and the applicability of design and evaluation for those populations.
reference_excerpt: To be eligible to participate in the usability testing, participants had to reside in Australia, have been affected by miscarriage (women, partners or family members), have a good understanding of English, have access to a computer with Zoom conferencing capabilities and be willing for the interview to be recorded for the purpose of transcribing the audio component at a later time.

description: Low turnout for usability testing reduced the number of participants from 27 interested individuals to only eight who completed testing.
justification: High nonresponse and inability to schedule interested participants constrained designers' capacity to evaluate designs with a broader sample, limiting iterative testing, discovery of usability issues, and confidence in saturation across user groups.
reference_excerpt: In total, 27 people completed an expression of interest form online. Of the 27 women, eight participated across the two rounds of testing... The remaining 19 women either did not respond to further communication about the testing session or were unable to attend the scheduled session times.

description: A revised layout was added late in the process and the team could not test that new layout with users.
justification: This prevented designers from evaluating whether the layout changes improved comprehension or navigation, hindering the 'evaluate designs' and 'integrate feedback & iteration' workloads.
reference_excerpt: In the last version (Supplementary file #2), these features were emphasised even more by isolating them on a separate cover page, but we could not test this new layout as it was added in the last version.

description: Pictograms were added only partially and inconsistently and the final pictogram set had not been evaluated with users.
justification: This limited the team's ability to iteratively refine visual design elements and assess whether pictograms supported navigation and comprehension (evaluate designs; integrate feedback).
reference_excerpt: These generated positive comments, but we did not use them systematically, nor consistently, and some participants found them unclear. In the last DBox template that has not yet been evaluated (Supplementary file #2), we systematically added pictograms specially designed by a graphic designer to illustrate ...

description: The need for the DBox to remain usable in black-and-white prevented implementing a more intuitive color-coded GRADE representation.
justification: This format constraint blocked a straightforward visual solution to improve clarity of evidence quality, hindering the team's ability to address comprehension issues (produce design solutions; evaluate designs).
reference_excerpt: One participant suggested using green, yellow and red instead of the ‘+’ for a more intuitive representation of the quality of the evidence. This idea was not implemented because the DBox needed to be usable in a black and white version.

description: Researchers did not have access to participants' medical records and had to rely on the moderator's qualitative classification of dementia severity.
justification: Lack of clinical records limited the team's objective understanding of users' clinical context, constraining the 'understand context of use' and 'manage user understanding' workloads.
reference_excerpt: We did not have access to their medical records, but the moderator—a registered nurse—qualitatively classified the severity of their dementia as moderate (n=9), severe (n=9) or very severe (n=5).

description: Navigation to access the glossary was challenging in the printable DBox format.
justification: Difficulty accessing definitions impeded designers' ability to ensure clarity of content for users, limiting the 'address holistic experience' and 'understand context of use' workloads and preventing effective iteration on glossary presentation.
reference_excerpt: The glossary proved essential for patient decision aids targeting older adults with dementia and their caregivers, but navigation to access it was a challenge.

description: Designers avoided using icon arrays because the DBox was designed as a printable PDF and icon arrays would lengthen the document.
justification: The printable format constraint prevented adoption of a risk-communication format that might have improved comprehension, hindering 'produce design solutions' and 'evaluate designs' workloads.
reference_excerpt: However, we did not use icon arrays, to avoid lengthening the DBox, which we designed as a printable pdf.

description: Some topics elicited strong emotional responses that were impossible to foresee and that lengthened the design process.
