justification: Unpredictable emotional reactions required additional iterations and tailoring, constraining the team's ability to plan and execute timely iterative testing (integrate feedback & iteration; manage user understanding).
reference_excerpt: Some topics may also elicit a very strong emotional response, which might be impossible to foresee and may lengthen the design process.

description: Presence of caregivers during sessions reduced spontaneity of both caregivers and patients, potentially biasing feedback.
justification: Dyad dynamics and caregiver dominance limited the research team's ability to facilitate authentic user involvement and collect unfiltered user input, hindering 'facilitate user involvement' and 'manage user understanding'.
reference_excerpt: However, caregivers may have been less spontaneous in some of their opinions because of the presence of the person in their care, and this could have influenced our conclusions. The presence of caregivers may also have caused some of the seniors with dementia to be less spontaneous, particularly if their caregivers played a dominant role in the dyad.

description: Some participants considered evidence, GRADE ratings and benefit/harm probabilities to be irrelevant and designers found no strategy in the template to address this belief.
justification: Users' misunderstanding or dismissal of evidence undermined designers' ability to manage user understanding and to specify content requirements that would both inform and engage users, limiting iteration effectiveness.
reference_excerpt: On the other hand, participants found some parts to be of little relevance, use or interest. A number of caregivers mentioned that the DBox was of no use to patients who could not participate in the decision-making process because of cognitive decline. ... Anyway, I mean this page, to be practical—page 4—the harms, I would take it out altogether. I would leave it up to the clinicians to read that. We have no use for the studies that’ve been done. (Caregiver #9, DBox #1) No strategy was found to address this in the DBox template.

description: Wording used to express priorities required several rounds of revision before arriving at acceptable phrasing.
justification: Repeated rewording increased the number of evaluation cycles and consumed design resources, hindering 'specify user requirements' and 'integrate feedback & iteration' workloads.
reference_excerpt: The wording used to express priorities required several rounds before we were able to arrive at the best expression, which suggests that the list of priorities would benefit from the input from a patient/caregiver expert panel.

description: One DBox (power of attorney) required major content additions between rounds, which temporarily lowered user satisfaction until further redesign in a subsequent round.
justification: Topic-specific complexity forced substantial late-stage revisions and extra testing rounds, limiting efficiency of iteration and delaying stabilization of the template (integrate feedback & iteration; evaluate designs).
reference_excerpt: In the current study, the DBox on the power of attorney required adding much information on the various legal options in the second round, generating lower scores before the table comparing the various options and their features were incorporated in the third round.

description: Pre-prepared stress scripts were perceived by teens as inauthentic and even 'insulting', forcing researchers to abandon them and ask teens to craft their own stories.
justification: This negative reaction undermined trust and authenticity, hindering the researchers' ability to manage user understanding and to facilitate authentic participation and iteration in role-play interaction studies.
reference_excerpt: However, the first time we presented this script, a few teens immediately commented in writing on the script that they found this script was “insulting” and “fake.” Although based in teen data, our script did not meet the teens’ need for an authentic story during role play and interaction.

description: Creating relationships with stakeholders and users in participatory research was time consuming, limiting how quickly researchers could engage and iterate.
justification: The time-intensive nature of relationship-building constrained the team's capacity to facilitate user involvement at scale and to sustain ongoing user-centred iteration and evaluation activities.
reference_excerpt: First, as is often true in participatory research, the process of creating relationships with stakeholders and users can be time consuming.

description: Conducting studies 'in the wild' introduced many uncontrollable situations that could cause studies to fail despite researcher flexibility.
justification: Unpredictable field conditions impeded the team's ability to reliably plan and execute user research, which hindered understanding context of use, conducting evaluations, and performing iterative design cycles.
reference_excerpt: Second, conducting studies in the wild provides huge benefits for contextual validity, but also allows for an unlimited number of uncontrollable situations. Maintaining flexibility within design can be helpful, but even then there is still potential for studies to fail in the wild.

description: Communicating and disseminating novel participatory methods to the engineering community was difficult and time intensive.
justification: This external communication burden limited the team's ability to coordinate multidisciplinary collaboration and to integrate participatory-method feedback into broader engineering practices, slowing adoption and iterative refinement across stakeholders.
reference_excerpt: Finally, although often much appreciated, communicating and disseminating new, participatory iterations of commonly used methods to an engineering community can be difﬁcult and time intensive.

description: Direct input (writing) in VR proved technically difficult, forcing the team to redesign the interaction to avoid in-VR text entry. This constraint required changing prototype mechanics and interaction metaphors.
justification: The difficulty with writing in VR impeded the team's ability to produce and iterate on design solutions and prototypes, affecting 'produce design solutions' and 'integrate feedback & iteration' workloads.
reference_excerpt: Immediately we learned that writing in VR was a complicated task, leading us to the design of a tree of negative thoughts from which teens could collect leaves and burn them in a nearby fire.

description: The study had a small sample of teen participants and the team was unable to test for effectiveness. This limited sample constrained their capacity to evaluate intervention outcomes.
justification: A small participant sample and inability to test effectiveness directly limited the designers' ability to evaluate designs and manage evolving user understanding through longitudinal testing, hindering 'evaluate designs' and 'manage user understanding' workloads.
reference_excerpt: Our current work was limited due to our small sample of teens and our inability to test for effectiveness.

description: No prior immersive implementations of a visual analog scale existed, requiring the team to develop a new in-VR measurement tool. The novelty increased design and development burden for assessment.
justification: Lack of existing immersive VAS tools constrained the designers' ability to evaluate and measure user states reliably within VR, hindering the 'evaluate designs' and 'specify user requirements' workloads.
reference_excerpt: While some recent work [19] has explored multiple-choice style questionnaires in VR, no immersive tools has been developed using visual analog scale.

description: COVID-19 restrictions forced all interviews to be conducted remotely via Zoom, biasing participation toward technologically literate stakeholders and limiting in-person engagement.
justification: Remote-only interviews constrained the designers' ability to facilitate broad user involvement and to understand context of use through in-person observation, reducing the representativeness of user understanding and potentially limiting requirements specification and iteration.
reference_excerpt: Because of ongoing COVID-19 restrictions on in-person engagements, interviews were conducted via the UCSF Zoom video platform (Zoom Video Communications, Inc) ... All interviews were conducted remotely, using the UCSF Zoom video platform, which may have biased the patient stakeholders to people who are technologically literate and have access to the internet.

description: Qualitative analysis was conducted with the interviewer serving as the sole coder, introducing risk of analytic bias in interpreting stakeholder feedback.
justification: Relying on a single coder impeded the team's ability to robustly synthesize and triangulate user insights, which hinders managing user understanding, integrating feedback and iteration, and specifying reliable user requirements.
reference_excerpt: Although the interviewer was the sole coder, the stakeholder advisory team provided ongoing consultation on the coding scheme and how to code less frequently occurring responses. Finally, having the interviewer serve as the primary coder could have introduced bias into the qualitative analysis process.

description: Participant sampling was limited to clinicians at UCSF and patients seen by that group, which may have omitted important feedback from a wider cohort of users.
justification: This recruitment scope constrained designers' ability to manage user understanding and validate generalizability, limiting their capacity to specify requirements and ensure the tool fits diverse contexts of use.
reference_excerpt: Only clinicians at UCSF and patients seen by this (broad) group of clinicians were interviewed; therefore, we may have missed important feedback from a wider cohort of users.

description: Integration and scalability of the tool to other health systems depended on each system's internal governance and motivation, posing an external organizational constraint.
justification: This external dependence limited the designers' ability to plan and execute scalable implementations and to coordinate multidisciplinary adoption across health systems, hindering the operational workload of producing deployable solutions and integrating them into varied clinical workflows.
reference_excerpt: However, successful integration into other health systems depends on the internal governance and motivation within each system.

description: Collected wearable data are largely inaccessible for visualization or integration within clinic EHRs, limiting availability of patient-generated data streams.
justification: Inaccessible wearable data prevented designers from integrating important data sources into the tool, constraining their ability to specify requirements, produce design solutions that incorporate multimodal PGD, and evaluate designs with realistic data inputs.
reference_excerpt: However, most of the collected wearable data remain inaccessible for visualization or integration within a clinic’s EHR. This limitation can impede the effective use of PGD by clinicians and compromise patient-physician collaboration related to PGD [52].

description: Research ethics board (IRB) requirements and timelines constrained the iterative, discovery-driven research methods designers rely on.
justification: Requiring pre-specified methods, larger sample sizes, and submission many months in advance prevented designers from adapting inquiry during fieldwork, hindering managing user understanding, iterative learning, and studying context of use.
reference_excerpt: Initial IRB feedback stated that A360 did not have an adequate sample size and had to change the wording of questions and limit their methods to a specific set of 9 approaches. The requirement to submit the design research plan 6 to 9 months in advance of project launch also limited the design team’s ability to adapt their methods as needed throughout the process.

description: Funder-imposed short timelines and fixed budget allocations limited the time and flexibility needed for HCD’s iterative prototyping and co-creation.
justification: Donor preferences for short-term results and initial allocation of short timelines prevented adequate iteration and pivoting, impeding integration of feedback & iteration, coordination with stakeholders, and implementation of refined solutions.
reference_excerpt: While the donor originally allocated funding for an 8-month timeline, the project ultimately took 24 months for several reasons... once the timeline began to get delayed, amendments to the pre-defined project plan and budget took additional time. ... funders preferred shorter-term TA projects and near-term results, while governments wanted several years of TA.

description: Lack of mutual understanding and experience with HCD between the design team and implementing partners created confusion about roles and ways of working.
justification: The need to orient partners unfamiliar with HCD disrupted collaboration, undermining the designers’ ability to coordinate multidisciplinary teams, facilitate stakeholder involvement, and sustain aligned processes during implementation.
reference_excerpt: In Reimagining TA, no such start-up phase was built in for Sonder and JSI to align on process and approach. The design team had to orient the JSI team to the HCD methodology and approach while simultaneously kicking off activities in-country... This created confusion, mutual questioning of the project approach, and a lack of clarity around roles and responsibilities.

description: Insufficient or superficial government buy-in and inconsistent stakeholder attendance limited true co-creation and local ownership.
justification: Governments accepting initiatives without deep engagement or competing priorities reduced stakeholder participation and commitment, hindering designers’ ability to facilitate user involvement, integrate feedback, and ensure sustainable implementation.
reference_excerpt: Given the limited timeline for securing government buy-in, the government accepted the initiative without full awareness of and commitment to the level of engagement needed for a true co-creation process... In Nigeria, inconsistent stakeholder engagement in the workshops resulted in fragmented insights and low commitment to the process and the solutions.

description: Procurement realities of government/U.S. government supply chains constrained the ability to translate prototypes into scalable program materials.
justification: Requirements for competitive contracting and specific procurement mechanisms impeded transitioning prototypes to implementation, limiting the designers’ ability to produce and deploy design solutions at scale.
reference_excerpt: The prototypes of the V starter kits and distribution plans developed in South Africa were not automatically transferable to a new context given the procurement realities of supplying large, U.S. government-funded programs. Ultimately, implementing V in Zimbabwe required procurement through an existing U.S. government supply chain mechanism... which required a competitive contracting process.

description: Project timelines and budgets did not allow time or resources to build HCD capacity among in-country partners.
justification: Without dedicated time and funding for capacity building, designers could not embed design skills in partners, which hindered sustaining adaptive management, continuing iteration, and implementing solutions after core design support ended.
reference_excerpt: For Reimagining TA, given timeline and budget constraints, there was no time to build the HCD skills of in-country co-creation team members. Therefore, the solutions identified have not been implemented systematically.

description: Practical and cost constraints prevented launching an independent impact evaluation for V, limiting rigorous assessment of design-led outcomes.
justification: Challenges in identifying a sufficiently rigorous methodology at feasible cost blocked designers from conducting an impact evaluation, hindering their ability to evaluate designs and generate evidence to persuade stakeholders to adopt HCD approaches.
reference_excerpt: For V, an independent impact evaluation failed to launch due to challenges in identifying a sufficiently rigorous methodology at a feasible cost. The evaluation of V in Zimbabwe was therefore designed to leverage existing, routine program monitoring systems.

description: The COVID-19 pandemic paused implementation activities, interrupting planned testing and scaling of HCD solutions.
justification: Pandemic-related pauses prevented timely prototyping, testing, and iteration, directly constraining designers’ ability to integrate feedback, evaluate solutions, and sustain momentum toward implementation.
reference_excerpt: In 2019, USAID engaged the Engage Design consortium... to adapt V for program implementation. Due to COVID-19, implementation was paused but has recently resumed, with results expected in late 2021.

description: Clinical encounter routines and opening questions caused information about patients' life context to emerge haphazardly, limiting researchers' ability to observe natural disclosures in clinic visits.
justification: This organizational/human-environment constraint hindered designers' ability to manage user understanding and to study the context of use because relevant life information did not surface reliably during observations.
reference_excerpt: First, information about patients’ capacity and context sometimes arose naturally, but haphazardly throughout the visit. Patients who spoke freely and enjoyed talking about their life upon meeting them, changed completely during the encounter. There, they spoke only of their medical conditions and immediate concerns, and none of the life issues they had mentioned to us previously.

description: Existing assessment data (questionnaires) completed by patients were not reviewed or discussed in encounters, preventing designers from using those data to inform understanding.
justification: Because completed assessments were ignored in practice, researchers could not rely on them to specify user requirements or understand context of use, limiting their ability to integrate feedback into design decisions.
reference_excerpt: Assessments that offered insights about the patient’s capacity were not used for this purpose. For example, in one encounter, the patient had filled out multiple questionnaires, one regarding depression, one regarding anxiety, and one regarding alcohol consumption. Despite being available during the encounter, these were never reviewed or discussed.

description: Patient advisory group members initially found the concept of clinicians asking about coping unfamiliar, which limited their immediate engagement with the design idea.
justification: This lack of familiarity among users hindered designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and to manage user understanding during co-design activities, requiring additional effort to introduce and explain the concept.
reference_excerpt: At first, participants struggled with this concept; it was clearly foreign to them, even after years of living with chronic conditions.

description: The terminology researchers initially used to describe patient capacity was more suitable to researchers and clinicians than to patients, necessitating rewording to enable patient participation.
justification: This communication/terminology mismatch impeded designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and to specify user requirements until language was made patient-friendly.
reference_excerpt: The words that we used to describe patient capacity (Physical, Emotional, Personal, Financial, Social, and Environmental) were friendlier to researchers and physicians than to patients. To fully allow patients to participate, these needed to be reconsidered.

description: Older patients struggled with the prototypes' color contrast, forcing designers to change the visual design to a high-contrast black-and-white version.
justification: This usability/accessibility issue required designers to revise design solutions and iterate further, directly affecting the produce design solutions and integrate feedback & iteration workloads.
reference_excerpt: We learned from stakeholder feedback, that older patients struggled with the color contrast and preferred a highly contrasted, black-and-white version.

description: Using a mock-up instead of a fully functional prototype limited functionality and required extra interviewer support, preventing observation of natural user interactions and impairing evaluation of the values clarification exercise.
justification: This methodological/resource constraint hindered the designers' ability to evaluate designs and integrate feedback because it stopped them observing real user behavior and produced glitches that distorted usability and comprehension testing.
reference_excerpt: First, asking users to review a mock-up instead of a finished product requires much more involvement from the interviewer, which prevented us from observing real user interaction with the web-based decision aid. ... However, the mock-up functionality was limited and caused some unintended glitches. ... the mock-up clearly impaired understanding of the values clarification exercise.

description: Difficulty recruiting participants due to reliance on health care providers and the vulnerability of the target population resulted in small, non-diverse samples and constrained quantitative evaluation.
justification: External stakeholder gatekeeping and population vulnerability limited the designers' ability to facilitate user involvement, manage evolving user understanding across diverse subgroups, and evaluate designs quantitatively (e.g., preventing statistical testing and broader sampling).
reference_excerpt: As we experienced challenges recruiting participants with this strategy, we also invited people with MCI who were registered in a Quebec database managed by one of us (CH). ... The vulnerability of the population made it hard to recruit subjects with the help of HCPs, as they wanted to protect them from the hassles of a research project. Consequently, we had to rely on alternative strategies to recruit older adults with MCI. We could not, therefore, diversify the participants who helped at each evaluation round, for example, for levels of MCI, educational background, and technology skills.

description: Participants often reported that they understood the content even when interviewers observed misunderstandings, making it difficult for researchers to elicit genuine difficulties through self-report alone.
justification: This interactional/emotional issue impeded managing user understanding and evaluating designs because designers could not rely on direct participant comments and had to depend on more involved observational and teach-back methods to surface true usability problems.
reference_excerpt: Second, having the users communicate their difficulties was not always easy because they generally felt that they understood the content even when it was clear to the interviewer that they had not.

description: Only a single round of usability testing with a relatively small sample limited the team's ability to iteratively evaluate and refine the design.
justification: This resource constraint prevented adequate integration of feedback and iteration and limited the designers' capacity to evaluate designs with a sufficiently diverse user sample.
reference_excerpt: One of the limitations of this work is that the design requirements and evaluations were conducted with intended users from various representative underserved communities in South Texas and the result may not generalize to all underserved populations. In addition, only one round of usability testing was conducted with a relatively small sample of representative users and nurse educators.

description: The design process excluded physicians from stakeholder feedback, leaving provider perspectives incomplete.
justification: Omission of this external stakeholder group reduced access to provider domain knowledge and constrained the designers' ability to manage user/stakeholder understanding and to specify requirements affecting clinical workflows.
reference_excerpt: The focus group was only made up of diabetes educators; however, in the future, feedback from physicians will be requested.

description: Participant recruitment was geographically limited to underserved communities in South Texas, restricting the representativeness of findings.
justification: This contextual limitation impeded the designers' ability to manage evolving, generalizable user understanding and to specify user requirements applicable to broader underserved populations.
reference_excerpt: One of the limitations of this work is that the design requirements and evaluations were conducted with intended users from various representative underserved communities in South Texas and the result may not generalize to all underserved populations.

description: Existing biases toward certain platforms, functionality, or systems posed challenges for deriving platform-independent requirements.
justification: This environmental bias hindered the designers' ability to specify unbiased, platform-agnostic user requirements and threatened the fidelity of initial design specifications.
reference_excerpt: One of the notable challenges in digital health design is the bias in requirements toward certain platforms, functionality, and/or existing systems.

description: Hospital privacy and security requirements forced removal of cancer-specific content and prevented in-app note storage, constraining designers' ability to provide tailored features.
justification: This organizational constraint limited designers' ability to specify user requirements and address the holistic user experience by preventing features that required higher privacy (eg, diagnosis-specific content or personal notes), thereby constraining design decisions and potential iterations.
reference_excerpt: For example, one security concern was that if the intervention mentioned diagnoses (eg, cancer), this could compromise user privacy. Another option was to completely avoid the word cancer and any cancer-specific information in the app. Based on user input and security recommendations, it was decided to choose the second option and not include diagnosis-specific information.

description: Usability testing included a limited number of participants, restricting the designers' ability to robustly evaluate the prototype with diverse users.
justification: The small sample size constrained the evaluation workload and the team's capacity to manage evolving user understanding and to reliably integrate feedback across varied user groups.
reference_excerpt: Second, the usability testing included a limited number of participants, which is, however, not uncommon for iterative design processes [49].

description: Usability testing covered all functionalities but did not test all content sentences, leaving portions of content unvalidated with users.
justification: By not evaluating all content, designers were limited in their ability to fully evaluate designs and integrate feedback for content-level refinement, potentially missing issues affecting comprehension and engagement.
reference_excerpt: First, usability testing involved all functionalities but not all content sentences.

description: Participant recruitment relied on a convenience sample from hospital and social-media invitations, introducing selection bias among interviewed users.
justification: This recruitment approach limited the designers' ability to manage comprehensive user understanding and to ensure requirements represented the broader target population, constraining specification of user requirements and iteration priorities.
reference_excerpt: Cancer survivors participating in the user interviews responded to hospital or social media-related invitations and represented a sample of convenience, which can introduce selection bias.

description: User testing was limited to a very small sample of survivors (n=4), restricting the breadth of end-user input available to the design team.
justification: This constrained designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and evaluate designs with a representative set of users, limiting management of user understanding and iterative refinement based on diverse feedback.
reference_excerpt: First, user testing was performed by only 4 survivors of breast cancer. However, the original StressProffen intervention was developed with user input, enabling user testing of primarily new exercises in the 2 new versions.

description: Only newly developed content was user-tested; previously tested original content was not re-evaluated within the adapted versions.
justification: By restricting testing to only new exercises, designers were limited in their ability to evaluate the full adapted interventions and to manage comprehensive user understanding of the complete program and context of use.
reference_excerpt: As the original StressProffen content has already been user tested by survivors of cancer as well as health care providers [22], only new, developed content was user tested in the 2 new versions.

description: Pandemic restrictions forced several workshops to be conducted digitally, which may have affected the development process and team interactions.
justification: Remote workshops could impede coordination of the multidisciplinary team and the ease of iterative content development and feedback integration, hindering collaboration and shared decision-making workloads.
reference_excerpt: Third, some of the adaption and development of program content were conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, meaning that several workshops had to be conducted digitally due to pandemic restrictions. This could potentially have impacted the development process.

description: The mindfulness-based (MBI) version ended up with more text, more steps, and longer audio than the CBT (CBI) version, making exact equivalence between versions difficult to achieve.
justification: This methodological/content constraint limited designers' ability to specify identical user requirements and to fully control non-theoretical confounds, affecting workloads for specifying requirements and addressing the holistic experience across versions.
reference_excerpt: Findings show how this goal was primarily achieved, despite the final MBI-version being slightly longer, with more steps and total words and auditory length compared to the final CBI-version, and the CBI-version having more exercises compared to the MBI-version.

description: The number of participants in some studies was relatively small, limiting the breadth of empirical input available to the design team.
justification: Small sample sizes constrain designers' ability to manage user understanding and understand the context of use because fewer participant perspectives reduce the diversity and confidence of user insights used to specify requirements and inform iteration.
reference_excerpt: First, the number of participants of some studies was relatively small.

description: More healthcare professionals than patients were interviewed, producing an imbalance in stakeholder input.
justification: This sampling imbalance limits designers' capacity to accurately manage user understanding and specify user requirements for patients, because patient perspectives were underrepresented relative to professional viewpoints during synthesis and value specification.
reference_excerpt: Second, it may be noted that more healthcare professionals were interviewed than patients, but this is mostly because we included a wide range of healthcare professionals such as nurses, general practitioners, cardiologists, lifestyle coaches, etc.

description: Healthcare professionals reported they neither have time nor receive reimbursements to keep track of current eHealth developments, making engagement burdensome.
justification: Limited time and lack of reimbursement among external stakeholders hinder designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and coordinate with clinical stakeholders, reducing opportunities for iterative feedback and validation within routine care settings.
reference_excerpt: healthcare professionals expressed the wish to receive an overview of eHealth applications to promote healthy living, they neither have time nor receive reimbursements to keep track of current developments.

description: Personas used to derive requirements were not yet validated and remain to be confirmed in practice.
justification: Unvalidated personas represent a lack of validated user knowledge, constraining designers' ability to specify user requirements and confidently produce design solutions and evaluate whether prototypes match real user archetypes.
reference_excerpt: Finally, the developed personas that were needed to work out the eHealth requirements and customer journey were mostly based on stakeholder interviews. Now that the PHA is ready for use in cardiac rehabilitation, persona validation will be the next step.

description: Predefined project goals constrained design scope by requiring Bolster to be a self-guided mobile intervention, limiting the incorporation of features that required clinical or synchronous social support.
justification: These a priori constraints imposed by the project limited the team's ability to translate user feedback into certain design solutions (eg, expert Q&A or peer forums), hindering the workloads of specifying user requirements and producing design solutions that users requested.
reference_excerpt: Design objectives for Bolster were constrained to some extent by predefined project goals. Bolster was a priori proposed as a self-guided mobile intervention. Thus, caregiver feedback related to intervention features that could require clinical support (eg, an expert question-and-answer feature) or social features (eg, peer forums) was incorporated into Bolster in a manner consistent with these a priori constraints (eg, providing clinician videos rather than synchronous communication and links to support websites rather than the development of new tools).

description: Recruitment primarily via internet channels produced a sample likely predisposed to digital tools and drawn from small groups, limiting representativeness.
justification: This recruitment strategy constrained the team's ability to manage user understanding and to study the full context of use across diverse caregiver populations, reducing confidence in requirements and generalizability of findings.
reference_excerpt: First, our user-centered development process was meant to solicit detailed guidance from caregivers with lived experience; study conclusions are drawn from small samples and may not generalize to all members of this population. Furthermore, given the fact that recruitment occurred primarily on the internet, participants may be drawn from a population that is already predisposed to digital tools.

description: The field trial was brief (1 week) and included study-team outreach to encourage use, which likely altered natural usage patterns.
justification: These trial conditions limited the team's ability to evaluate the intervention under real-world deployment, hindering the workload of evaluating designs and integrating realistic user feedback for iteration and longer-term use planning.
reference_excerpt: Third, field trial results may speak primarily to caregiver experiences during a test period rather than the real-world deployment of Bolster. Participants were likely motivated to provide helpful feedback, and this likely affected their frequency of use of the intervention, particularly given the fact that the field trial lasted just 1 week. Interactions with the study team also likely encouraged use. This is particularly the case given the fact that participants received outreach to ensure that the app was functioning.

description: There were no additional contacts with participants for repeat interviews or feedback on findings after initial sessions.
justification: Lack of follow-up contact prevented iterative engagement with participants, constraining the team's ability to integrate feedback and perform iterative cycles of refinement based on longitudinal user input.
reference_excerpt: Participants were compensated with US $75 gift cards for their time. There were no additional contacts with participants for repeat interviews or feedback on findings.

description: Baseline ceiling effects on the illness-knowledge measure (KAST) limited sensitivity to detect changes in knowledge.
justification: This measurement limitation constrained the designers' and researchers' ability to evaluate intervention effects on illness knowledge, hindering the evaluation workload and interpretation of whether design changes achieved knowledge-related targets.
reference_excerpt: Notably, illness knowledge scores seemed to be affected by ceiling effects because many participants received a high score on the KAST at baseline (mean 16.72 correct out of 20 compared with psychometric work on the initial development of the KAST [49] suggesting typical average scores among family members of 10.9 out of 20 or among lay community members of 9.3 out of 20).

description: Data collection was conducted without audio recordings, which reduced data quality and depth available to researchers.
justification: The absence of audio recordings limited designers' ability to manage user understanding and to evaluate and verify user feedback post-hoc, hindering in-depth qualitative insight and rigorous assessment of participant responses.
reference_excerpt: Especially working without audio recordings likely has affected data quality and data depth.

description: The team had difficulty recruiting participants with lower education backgrounds, limiting sample diversity.
justification: This recruitment constraint hindered designers' ability to gain a representative understanding of the target population and impaired requirements specification and contextual understanding for less-educated user segments.
reference_excerpt: While a heterogeneous age distribution was achieved, it was especially challenging to recruit participants with a lower education background.

description: Refugees were not pre-screened for symptoms of distress, so participants may not have matched the app's intended clinical target group.
justification: Not sampling the intended clinical population constrained the designers' ability to specify accurate user requirements and to evaluate the prototype's suitability and potential health impact for the actual target users.
reference_excerpt: In addition, the interviewed refugees were not pre-screened for symptoms of distress. Consequently, the feedback does not necessarily originate from the exact target group of the app (i.e., Syrian refugees with increased distress and impaired functioning).

description: The team used prototyping software rather than a fully functioning app, so interactive exercises and real use could only be simulated.
justification: Relying on non-functional prototypes limited designers' ability to evaluate interactive features, observe real user behaviour over time, and integrate realistic usability feedback into iteration cycles.
reference_excerpt: Since the prototyping software was used instead of providing a functioning version of an actual app, certain elements such as the interactive exercises could only be simulated at this stage. In order to receive actual feedback on a working prototype it will be necessary to provide access to a fully functioning version.

description: Free-list interviews asked respondents to answer for the community, causing some responses to be given as representatives rather than from personal experience.
justification: This interactional method choice produced secondary/hearsay data that weakened designers' ability to manage deep, personal user understanding and to accurately characterise contexts of use.
reference_excerpt: In the free list interviews, respondents still answered as representatives of the larger group instead of from a personal standpoint. Consequently, this approach may have introduced themes that were rather based on hearsay than on personal experience.

description: The planned contact-on-demand e-helper model included a 48-hour response latency that was judged too long and required more efficient e-helper management.
justification: Operational constraints around e-helper availability and response time limited designers' ability to define acceptable guidance features and specify feasible system requirements, impeding production of an acceptable support model.
reference_excerpt: the suggested response latency of up to 48 h was universally considered as too long and needs to be reduced, e.g., through more efficient systems for e-helper management.

description: Qualitative analysis was performed by a single reviewer, limiting analytic redundancy and rigor in deriving themes from interviews.
justification: Having only a solitary coder reduced the designers' capacity to robustly manage user understanding and to confidently translate insights into user requirements, hindering analysis and specification workloads.
reference_excerpt: A solitary reviewer analyzed the coding, which was validated through member checking of adolescent health and endocrinology specialists at SickKids Hospital.

description: The pilot used a single-site, small convenience sample with no control group, limiting the study's generalizability and the designers' ability to evaluate outcomes robustly.
justification: The limited sample and site constrained the designers' ability to evaluate the intervention and to generate generalizable evidence needed for iterative refinement and specifying broader user requirements.
reference_excerpt: The pilot was limited to a single-site, small convenience sample with no control group, which limited our ability to generalize the findings and determine the efficacy of the intervention fully.

description: Participant dropout and missing baseline meter data reduced the analyzable sample, undermining planned outcome analyses.
justification: Incomplete data and attrition directly hindered the designers' and researchers' ability to evaluate the design's effectiveness and to integrate evaluation findings into subsequent iterations.
reference_excerpt: Of these, 2 did not complete the full 12-week pilot study and 6 did not have sufficient baseline data from the meters for us to perform the analysis for the primary outcome measure.

description: Limited deployment and low/uneven engagement with the in-app community made it difficult to assess the social networking component's value.
justification: Insufficient scale and skewed participation constrained the designers' ability to evaluate the community feature with users, hindering evaluation and decisions about integrating social features into the product.
reference_excerpt: We also have few findings on the effect of the community aspect of the intervention, and its direct value is difficult to ascertain. Only through wider deployment can the use of these social networking aspects be properly evaluated.

description: The reward mechanism relied on iTunes redemption codes, raising concerns about the long-term sustainability of the incentive model.
justification: Sustainability constraints on the reward system limit the designers' ability to plan long-term deployment and iterative refinement of gamification features, affecting both design solution production and future evaluation.
reference_excerpt: The long-term sustainability of using iTunes redemption codes as a reward is an issue that requires attention.

description: Participant sampling was biased toward computer-literate young people who already had easy access to smartphones, limiting the designers' exposure to less tech-savvy or non-smartphone users.
justification: This participation bias constrained designers' ability to manage evolving user understanding and to study the full context of use and requirements for users without smartphone access, reducing the validity of requirements and potential design adaptations for those groups.
reference_excerpt: Our user groups were diverse, even though relatively small, with participating patients having different JIA subtypes at various stages of their treatment and from different ethnical backgrounds. The app’s design and evaluation were not affected by the characteristics of YP, but participation bias may have influenced the themes that emerged from our FGDs and interviews. For example, all study participants were computer literate and had easy access to smartphones; whether further refinements of the app are necessary for patients who are less familiar with this technology needs to be established.

description: Health care professionals (HCPs) raised concerns about accessibility for all patients and the additional resources and time required to monitor and interpret patient-generated app data.
justification: These stakeholder constraints imposed limits on designers' ability to integrate the system into clinical workflows and specified requirements (eg, desktop version, data presentation), and they created resource-based barriers that affected specification of user requirements and coordination with clinical teams.
reference_excerpt: The HCPs also identified possible barriers to integration such as accessibility to all patients and demands for additional resources. For example, HCPs proposed that a desktop version of the app will be beneficial to allow access to YP without a mobile phone. In addition, HCPs were concerned about the additional time needed to monitor remote symptom deteriorations and interpret additional information collected from the app.

description: A project-level decision (driven by clinical workflow concerns) limited the study to non–real-time data monitoring, preventing designers from evaluating real-time monitoring functionality during this stage.
justification: The explicit choice not to monitor data in real time restricted the designers' ability to evaluate and iterate on features that depend on real-time monitoring, thereby hindering design evaluation and integration testing in realistic clinical use contexts.
reference_excerpt: Therefore, before downloading the app, participants will be informed that data will not be monitored in real time for this stage of the project but will be reviewed during clinic consultations. This is also explicitly explained on the app with a disclosure statement.

description: Working with a multidisciplinary team increased process complexity and slowed system development because the team needed to reach a common understanding.
justification: This organizational/time constraint hindered the designers' ability to coordinate a multidisciplinary team and slowed integration of feedback and iterative development cycles.
reference_excerpt: As drawback, user involvement in all the development stages of an e-health system increases the complexity of the process. Working with a multidisciplinary team inevitably slows down system development due to the necessity of reaching a common understanding.

description: User contributions were often dismissed during the implementation process by stakeholders, causing misalignment between the system and healthcare delivery.
justification: This attitudinal barrier from implementers prevented designers from ensuring that user input was integrated into implementation, undermining the ability to integrate feedback and address the holistic user experience.
reference_excerpt: User involvement in design and evaluation stages is common in the health domain, but user contributions are often dismissed in the implementation process what results in systems facing user refusal since they are not aligned enough to the healthcare delivery or present a limited usability.

description: Participants' low confidence and hesitancy to use the app without help limited independent user testing and required hands-on demonstrations by the research team.
justification: This interactional issue impeded facilitation of user involvement and evaluation activities because designers had to modify testing procedures (practical showing) rather than observe unaided use, reducing the validity and ease of iterative evaluation.
reference_excerpt: Would you know use AppNephro without prior help? Yes: 25% No: 0% I don’t know: 75% Since the previous survey concluded that the participants showed hesitant to test AppNephro without help, this stage began by performing a practical showing.

description: Reconciling diverse user desires with technological possibilities imposed limits on the cost-efficiency of the product, constraining design choices.
justification: These cost and technology constraints limited designers' ability to iterate freely, specify and implement extensive user requirements, and produce solutions that satisfy all stakeholder groups.
reference_excerpt: A further issue is the continuous reconciliation between desires, preferences and needs of different kind of users and technology that imposes limits on the cost-efficiency of the product. Involving users requires to agree on every decision on system development by establishing balances among user needs and desires, technology possibilities and costs.

description: Clinicians' limited availability and short meeting times prevented full participation in design sessions.
justification: This constrained facilitation of user involvement and coordination of the multidisciplinary team, limiting designers' ability to manage user understanding and integrate feedback across iterations.
reference_excerpt: Challenges included time constraints as meetings were scheduled for only 1 hour and not all clinicians could fully participate in all design sessions.

description: Not all user groups were directly involved in the design process, creating gaps in representation.
justification: Incomplete user representation hindered designers' ability to fully understand the context of use and specify comprehensive user requirements, risking missed inputs that affect design decisions and iteration.
reference_excerpt: Because not all groups of users were directly involved in the design of T3, it is possible that important input may have been missed.

description: The design team struggled to decide which information elements to include due to diverse user roles and information needs.
justification: This cognitive/decision-making difficulty impeded the specification of clear user requirements and the production of stable design solutions, prolonging iterative design activities.
reference_excerpt: A challenge of the HCD process was deciding which information elements to include on T3, especially given the various users and roles with different information needs.

description: Nursing leadership concerns about the accuracy and safety of displayed information forced the team to add a proactive risk analysis step and raised issues about EHR data reliability and timely access.
justification: Stakeholder-driven requirements and data-source reliability constraints disrupted the planned HCD workflow and limited designers' ability to finalize requirements and iterate toward an implementable solution without resolving data/infrastructure dependencies.
reference_excerpt: We also discussed the impact of T3 on patient safety as nursing leaders expressed concern about the accuracy of the displayed information on T3. This led us to add a step in the HCD process and conduct a patient safety analysis (step 6).

description: Information-source reliability and timely access in the EHR were identified as important vulnerabilities for T3's data.
justification: Concerns about where data come from and EHR reliability constrained designers' ability to produce and evaluate an implementation-ready design, affecting specification of requirements and future integration/implementation work.
reference_excerpt: In a separate analysis, we found that about 90% of the information elements on T3 could be found in the EHR; the proactive risk analysis brought up the important issue of reliability of and timely access to information in the EHR.

description: The project produced and evaluated only a mock-up, so designers lacked information about real-world use of the technology.
justification: Absence of implementation prevented designers from conducting evaluation in actual workflow contexts, hindering the evaluate designs workload and the ability to refine designs based on real use.
reference_excerpt: Finally, because we developed and evaluated a technology mock-up, we do not have information on the actual use of the technology.

description: Fragmented and incomplete clinical information systems (EMR, lab, pharmacy, radiology, TB records) produced missing patient data that produced incorrect reminders.
justification: Poor system integration and missing data prevented the design team from producing accurate, actionable decision-support messages and hindered evaluation and iteration during usability testing and lab simulation.
reference_excerpt: Clinicians perceived the information systems, however helpful, to frequently suffer from missing patient data. Information system managers understood that this problem derived, in part, from the lack of integration between patient’s EMR, laboratory management information systems, pharmacy information systems, radiology information systems, and TB patient records.

description: Basic infrastructure and supply-chain limitations (lack of functional printers, unreliable electricity, limited radiology access, and IPT stock-outs) were identified as major implementation stumbling blocks.
justification: These external resource constraints directly impeded the team's ability to deliver, test, and scale the paper‑based decision support (production, deployment, and evaluation workloads) and forced the team to spend months addressing feasibility rather than design refinement.
reference_excerpt: These included technology systems requirements such as functional printers, reliable electricity, and improvements to EMR data quality and they also included clinical requirements such as adequate IPT stocks and supply-chain management, improved access to radiology, and provider knowledge of TB and IPT standards of care.

description: Most clinicians had insufficient knowledge about IPT eligibility and uncertainty about interpreting or ordering chest x-rays.
justification: Clinician knowledge gaps limited the team's ability to specify user requirements and design actionable reminders, because providers could not reliably act on or validate the system's recommendations during usability evaluation.
reference_excerpt: Clinician knowledge of IPT. Interview transcripts and observation sessions alike revealed that, although some clinicians were quite knowledgeable about global and institutional standards for determining IPT eligibility, most had insufficient knowledge to determine eligibility for their patients. In particular, they often described being unsure about the role of chest x-ray, when and if it should be ordered and how to read radiographs.

description: Clinicians were hesitant to initiate IPT for eligible patients due to prior experiences with drug 'stock-outs' and fear of contributing to drug resistance.
justification: This clinician reluctance reduced the actionability of reminders and hampered the team's ability to observe and iterate on real-world behavior change, affecting evaluation and integration of feedback.
reference_excerpt: Providers remained hesitant to start a patient on IPT due to pharmacy shortages. Previous experiences with periodic and long-term ‘‘stock-outs,’’ as participants described them, made clinicians wary of contributing toward drug resistance by exposing patients to IPT and not completing the regimen.

description: Operational data‑entry and record‑update processes were ineffective: providers' updates to patient records were not reliably entered into the EMR by the data team.
justification: Failure of the data workflow meant corrections from clinicians did not propagate into the system, producing persistent inaccurate reminders and preventing designers from validating fixes during iterative testing and evaluation.
reference_excerpt: "If I see the chest x-ray missing, first I ask the patient if they did it recently. If they say yes, then I ask what the result was. ... I make a note of it to update the information. And sometimes I repeat this note to the data team several times and nothing changes in the system. I keep getting the reminder."

description: Designers were unable to produce an initial functional prototype in the target magnesium alloy because the first prototype had to be manufactured in aluminum due to local access constraints. This limited their ability to test the design in the intended material early in the process.
justification: Requiring an aluminum prototype prevented designers from producing and evaluating solutions in the final material, hindering the 'produce design solutions' and 'evaluate designs' workloads (material-specific testing and iteration were deferred).
reference_excerpt: The first functional prototype is being manufactured in aluminum alloy, due to its ease of access in the local context. This prototype will be used to develop technical and usability tests. The resultant design will be prototyped in AZ31 magnesium alloy and the same tests mentioned will be applied.

description: Key manufacturing processes (surface treatments and powder metallurgy) were developed in parallel subprojects and had not been scaled for application, delaying their integration into the main design work. This separation constrained the team's ability to incorporate manufacturing solutions into the design on schedule.
justification: Because those processes were not yet scaled and integrated, the team could not finalize or test the magnesium prototype, hindering 'produce design solutions', 'integrate feedback & iteration', and coordination of the multidisciplinary team.
reference_excerpt: On the other hand, the processes for the treatment of the surfaces and the formation of pieces by powder metallurgy, were developed by materials engineers in parallel subprojects. The results of these subprojects will be integrated into the design process when said manufacturing processes are scaled for their application in the magnesium prototype.

description: Variation in how seniors execute gestures and differences in body types forced designers to collect more training samples than initially planned.
justification: This increased data-collection burden and constrained the designers' ability to train reliable activity-recognition models, hindering the operational workloads of understanding context of use and producing/evaluating design solutions.
reference_excerpt: During the training process one issue that required attention was the fact that users cannot execute the movements the same way. Moreover, the body type of each user was an issue that had to be resolved. For instance, some users are taller than others thus, the system would not have been able to identify the gestures and motions if it would have been trained based on a single person.

description: Existing literature guidance (three training users) proved insufficient for elderly participants, requiring empirical reassessment of sample-size needs.
justification: Relying on literature thresholds that did not transfer to this elderly population limited planners' ability to specify adequate training requirements and manage user-understanding and training procedures for the sensor algorithm.
reference_excerpt: Literature research indicated that the accepted number of people required in situations like this was three in order to cover all body types regarding weight and height. However, after testing that threshold using the live testing option provided by sensor’s SDK, it was noticed that system’s confidence level was below average.

description: Modeling the walking motion as a continuous gesture produced ambiguous stage transitions that the system misrecognized, forcing the team to abandon the initial approach and reclassify the motion as discrete.
justification: This technical and modeling difficulty impeded the designers' ability to evaluate and iterate on interaction mechanics, constraining the integration of feedback and the production of robust gesture-detection solutions.
reference_excerpt: After testing the above scenario, cases were noticed where the system could not recognize the gesture correctly. Specifically, after the end of stage 2 and just before the start of stage 3, the user has both legs on the ground the same as at the end of the gesture which resulted some times in a conflict state, where the system would falsely consider that the motion was completed after stage 2 and right before stage 3. The result of this was for the player to stop moving from time to time which had a negative effect on the overall game experience. Thus, it was decided to reject this approach and classify this motion as discrete and use the same training technique as for the leaning gesture.

description: Seniors required expert instruction and domain support (physiotherapist/researcher presence) to use the system effectively during evaluation.
justification: Needing expert facilitation increased the resource and coordination burden on designers and limited independent user participation, hindering the workload of facilitating user involvement and conducting evaluations.
reference_excerpt: The evaluation of the game tool took place at the Elderly Protection Center in the city of Ptolemaida, Greece. ... during the whole process a physiotherapist was present for domain-specific support and a researcher for administration and technical support. As for the data from the effort expectancy category show that seniors didn’t find the system hard to use but only after they got the appropriate instructions from an expert since they didn’t have the knowledge to use the system from the beginning.

description: The study had a limited number of participants and a short evaluation timeframe, constraining the strength and generalizability of results.
justification: Small sample size and short duration limited the designers' ability to perform robust evaluations and iterative refinements based on longer-term user data, hindering evaluation and managing evolving user understanding.
reference_excerpt: Limitations of the current study are acknowledged. The limited number of participants and the short evaluation timeframe prevent the justification of more sound results.

description: The team did not perform usability testing of the prototype, preventing completion of formal evaluation activities.
justification: Not having conducted usability (heuristic) testing directly prevents designers from performing the 'evaluate designs' workload and from integrating empirical feedback into further iterations.
reference_excerpt: First, we have presented the design and development of an eCoach prototype (i.e., ProHealth eCoach) for activity coaching. However, we have not performed its usability testing for the heuristic evaluation of the eCoach prototype.

description: Technical and logistical constraints (poor internet connectivity, BLE battery life, budget and time limitations) limited the study's ability to conduct and scale HCD activities.
justification: These resource constraints hinder facilitating user involvement (remote workshops and data uploads), understanding context of use (reliable continuous monitoring), and evaluating prototypes in realistic settings.
reference_excerpt: Fourth, constraints, such as poor internet connectivity, battery lifetime due to BLE and background processing, budget, time plan, technological limitations should be overcome.

description: The chosen medical-grade activity sensor (MOX2–5) cannot classify certain activities (cycling, swimming, rowing, skiing), forcing manual questionnaire reporting.
justification: This technological limitation increased reliance on self-report questionnaires and limited designers' ability to fully understand context of use and collect objective activity data, complicating specification of requirements and evaluation.
reference_excerpt: The current version of the MOX2–5 activity sensor is not suitable for classifying activities into the following detailed activity classes: cycling, swimming, rowing, and skiing. Therefore, the participants must report them manually as questionnaire data in the latest version of the eCoach app.

description: Vendor/manufacturer variability and opaque changes in consumer device algorithms make consumer wearables unreliable for long-term clinical trials.
justification: External stakeholder practices (device manufacturers changing algorithms/sensors) limit designers' ability to select stable sensing platforms and thus hinder specifying robust data requirements and planning longitudinal evaluations.
reference_excerpt: Furthermore, it is never known when the manufacturer replaces the algorithms or sensors in the device, so it is tricky to do clinical trials with such devices (over longer durations).

description: The study did not evaluate the credibility, reliability, or effectiveness of the recommendation generation and its presentation.
justification: Without assessing recommendation credibility and effectiveness, designers cannot complete evaluation and iteration workloads needed to refine recommendation logic, visualization, and persuasive strategies.
reference_excerpt: Third, this study has not evaluated recommendation generation’s credibility, reliability, and effectiveness and its presentation (direct and indirect) towards motivational, behavioral change.

description: Integration, scalability, and validation in relevant/operational environments have not been performed, leaving the prototype untested at higher readiness levels.
justification: Lack of integration and scalability testing prevents designers from evaluating the system in realistic contexts of use, hindering evaluation, iteration, and readiness for broader deployment.
reference_excerpt: We have designed and developed an initial version of the eCoach prototype; however, integration and scalability testing must be performed in the production environment.

description: Health care providers (eg, nurses) were not included in the standardized usability questionnaire, preventing designers from capturing provider perspectives on the care-provider app.
justification: Excluding providers limited the team's ability to facilitate user involvement and evaluate the care-provider app, hindering the HCD workloads of facilitating user involvement and evaluating designs.
reference_excerpt: As iCARE was in the testing stage, and the main focus of this study was to test the experience of patients and the usability of the patient app, and therefore, we did not include health care providers (such as nurses) to complete the Health-ITUES.

description: The team developed the apps only for Android initially and deferred iOS compatibility until the Android version was stable, limiting platform coverage during design and testing.
justification: Limiting development to Android constrained the designers' ability to understand context of use and to involve and evaluate users on other major platforms (iOS), impeding the workloads of understanding context of use and evaluating designs across device contexts.
reference_excerpt: The patient app and care provider app were developed to be compatible with Android-based smartphones, as they are more popular and affordable in China [27]. We will also develop iCARE to be compatible on iOS-based smartphones once the app is identified as being stable in Android-based smartphones.

description: A blood glucose monitor was not distributed to diabetic participants in stage II, so the team could not test glucose-monitoring integration with the app.
justification: Lack of device distribution prevented designers from evaluating the app's integration with glucose devices and from fully understanding context of use for diabetic patients, hindering the evaluation of designs and understanding of context of use.
reference_excerpt: As the blood glucose monitor was not distributed to patients with diabetes (10/61 patients) in stage II testing, it was not available for testing the differences in this regard.

description: A substantial number of eligible patients (n=40) refused to participate due to lack of time, schedule conflicts, or lack of interest, reducing available user input.
justification: Participant refusal limited designers' ability to recruit and involve end users for task analysis and usability evaluation, hindering the HCD workloads of facilitating user involvement and evaluating designs.
reference_excerpt: There were 40 patients eligible for the study but refused to participate due to various reasons, such as lack of time, conflict of schedule, or simply being uninterested.

description: Designers lacked control over the implementation of the third-party FatSecret app, constraining how the companion app could integrate and navigate across apps.
justification: This external dependency limited the designers' ability to manage cross-app navigation and to produce seamless design solutions and integrations required for effortless logging (process-level: manage user understanding; operational-level: produce design solutions, understand context of use).
reference_excerpt: While we lack control over the implementation of the FatSecret app, users can navigate backward using the built-in back navigation feature on both iOS and Android devices.

description: The FatSecret API did not provide timestamps for self-monitored data, forcing the research team to append timestamps in their backend to obtain the instrumentation needed for the adaptive intervention.
justification: This API limitation created additional engineering work and constrained designers' ability to straightforwardly gather temporally precise data necessary for specifying user requirements and for supporting the adaptive trigger algorithm (operational-level: specify user requirements; process-level: integrate feedback & iteration).
reference_excerpt: In addition, the FatSecret API does not include timestamps for self-monitored weight, caloric intake, or physical activity. However, the inclusion of timestamps is crucial for supporting the implementation and evaluation of our adaptive weight maintenance intervention... Thus, in our backend system, we appended timestamps to the data collected in FatSecret and BodyTrace when requesting data from those applications’ servers.

description: Delays in data synchronization between MyTrack+ and FatSecret disrupted expected real-time integration during pilot testing.
justification: Synchronization delays impeded evaluation and understanding of real-world use (operational-level: evaluate designs; process-level: manage user understanding and facilitate user involvement), requiring backend changes and limiting accurate assessment of the dual-app experience.
reference_excerpt: Notably, nearly all participants expressed concerns regarding the delay in data synchronization between MyTrack+ and FatSecret. To address this issue, we modified our Cloud Functions to request data from FatSecret’s server whenever the companion app is refreshed, effectively achieving G1.

description: The team used convenience sampling of university students for early usability testing instead of target users, which risked producing non-representative feedback and a local optimum design.
justification: Recruiting non-target participants limited designers' ability to manage evolving, accurate user understanding and to validate designs under realistic conditions (process-level: manage user understanding; operational-level: evaluate designs), potentially biasing iterative changes.
reference_excerpt: Although Computer Science students were not our main target users, according to Nielsen (49), involving students in the domain of interest from a local university in usability testing can still yield valuable feedback. We chose to recruit students as convenience samples (50) because (1) they are easier to reach and more readily available and (2) they could also be potential users of weight management apps.

description: The team did not perform a comprehensive analysis of semi-structured interviews and usability questionnaire responses, limiting the depth of evaluation and learning from pilot data.
justification: This omission constrained the designers' ability to integrate feedback, perform rigorous evaluation, and derive generalizable design requirements (process-level: integrate feedback & iteration; operational-level: evaluate designs; specify user requirements).
reference_excerpt: Second, it is important to note that we did not perform a comprehensive analysis of the conversations in our semi-structured interviews and measures of usability from questionnaire responses.

description: Project priorities required trade-offs favoring trial instrumentation and speed over richer commercial-level features, constraining the scope of design improvements responsive to some user preferences.
justification: Prioritizing the clinical trial's progress limited the team's ability to address broader user expectations and add more comprehensive functionality, reducing their capacity to address holistic experience and to produce broader design solutions (process-level: address holistic experience; operational-level: produce design solutions).
reference_excerpt: Not meeting these expectations may impact the app's usability, but trade-offs were necessary to achieve our main design goal: effectively supporting the implementation of our team’s specific adaptive weight intervention and prioritizing the progress of our clinical trial aimed at evaluating the intervention’s effectiveness.

description: Participant availability and scheduling conflicts reduced attendance across iterative testing rounds, limiting consistent user involvement.
justification: Irregular attendance and postponed/cancelled sessions prevented designers from conducting repeated evaluations with the same users, hindering facilitate user involvement and integrate feedback & iteration workloads.
reference_excerpt: Not all individuals participated in all rounds of testing for reasons related to doctor or dentist appointments, day trips, and availability of the residents. Consistent with other studies [62], we also experienced user testing sessions being postponed or canceled if the resident was ill or had a medical appointment and scheduled for other activities, and residents often felt too lethargic to engage in PA after lunch;

description: Residents' multiple physical, sensory, and cognitive impairments complicated recruitment, retention, and data collection activities.
justification: Health, sensory, and cognitive limitations among participants constrained the team's ability to manage user understanding, evaluate designs, and retain participants for iterative testing sessions.
reference_excerpt: Residents had multiple physical, sensory, and cognitive impairments. ... symptoms, including fatigue and hearing or visual impairments, which can severely impact all aspects of the research, especially recruitment, retention, and data collection [58].

description: A relatively small sample drawn from only two nursing homes limited the study's breadth and the designers' ability to generalize findings.
justification: Limited sample size and sites constrained the designers' ability to manage user understanding across diverse contexts and to confidently specify user requirements for broader deployments.
reference_excerpt: First, the study sample included a relatively small number of participants and included 2 mid- to large-sized nursing homes in Canada, which may impact the generalizability of the results to other contexts.

description: Technical development was time-consuming and relied on fragile hardware (single Arduino), slowing iteration and upgrades.
justification: Long programming times and fragile hardware limited the team's capacity to rapidly produce and refine design solutions and to iterate prototypes efficiently.
reference_excerpt: From a development perspective, the programming of the games was time consuming, and we found the single Arduino was fragile and hard to upgrade.

description: Having a member of the research team conduct some interviews may have inhibited participants from voicing negative feedback.
justification: Social desirability and reluctance to criticize the team reduced the accuracy of user feedback, hindering manage user understanding and integrate feedback & iteration activities.
reference_excerpt: Second, the interviewer for some of the interviews was a member of the research team, which may have prevented participants from sharing negative opinions that criticized the exergame.

description: Operational and acquisition costs in LTC settings limited the feasibility of technology adoption and broader deployments.
justification: Financial constraints and funding models restricted the designers' ability to plan for real-world implementation, scale testing, and to make design trade-offs informed by acquisition realities, affecting produce design solutions and evaluate designs in practice.
reference_excerpt: The primary barrier to the acquisition of new technology in LTC home adoption is cost. All the staff stakeholders identified cost as a barrier and explained how available funds were influenced by different variables, including home fundraising efforts, the annual funding envelope to support activities, and whether the payment model for the technology was an outright cost or a subscription-based service requiring ongoing payments.

description: Limited physical space in LTC homes and staff heavy workloads required designs to be lightweight, compact, and quick to set up.
justification: Spatial constraints and staff time pressures forced design trade-offs and constrained prototype form factors, hindering the designers' ability to explore alternative solutions and address holistic experience and produce design solutions workloads.
reference_excerpt: In addition, the lack of physical space was identified as an issue, so new interventions need to be adaptable to fit different-sized common areas and activity rooms. Staff also emphasized the need for the exergame design to be lightweight, compact, and quick to set up because of the heavy workloads.

description: A change in institutional isolation guidelines disrupted the study and evaluation activities, preventing planned quantitative analyses and complicating user testing.
justification: This organizational change hindered the designers' ability to evaluate prototypes and integrate feedback because frontline staff focused on guideline discrepancies rather than signage design, limiting the evaluation and iteration workload.
reference_excerpt: During this study, we were faced with the challenge of changing institutional guidelines for isolation precautions.
