This prevented a quantitative analysis of change in practice and presented a challenge during the evaluation with frontline staff, who were not yet familiar with the new guidelines and thus had a tendency to focus on the discrepancies between the "new" vs. the current guidelines, rather than signage design.

description: Safety and feasibility concerns (institutional/regulatory constraints) prevented implementation of some participant-ideated forcing-function solutions and forced designers to adopt less integrated prototypes.
justification: These external safety/feasibility constraints limited the team's ability to produce and test certain design solutions, constraining prototyping choices and iteration on potentially high-impact concepts.
reference_excerpt: During one workshop, participants working on the problem statement, "how might we ensure that required isolation measures are respected 100% of the time," ideated around forcing function solutions to detect if appropriate personal protective equipment had been donned prior to opening the patient door (Fig. 5). Due to safety and feasibility concerns with this idea, during the prototyping phase these participants instead employed masks suspended in the doorway through which healthcare providers must walk, thereby automatically donning a mask upon room entry.

description: The study used a very small sample (seven GM service leaders), limiting the breadth of user data available to the design team.
justification: Limited participant availability constrained the team's ability to evaluate designs and to manage a deep, generalizable understanding of end users, hindering evaluation and user-understanding workloads.
reference_excerpt: First, we performed our analysis with a sample size of seven GM service leaders. While this is a small number, this is within ai sample size that is common for qualitative, user experience, and participatory design research [26].

description: The team was unable to study the relationship between stakeholder engagement and organizational readiness for adopting GM services, creating an empirical knowledge gap.
justification: This lack of evidence prevented designers from fully understanding the context of use and from specifying user requirements that link stakeholder engagement to successful implementation, limiting requirements formation and contextual understanding.
reference_excerpt: Third, we were unable to study the relationship between stakeholder engagement and organizational readiness for a GM service or genetic test offering. The relationship between stakeholder engagement and quality improvement projects is supported by empirical findings of others [27], but more work remains to empirically study this relationship with GM services specifically.

description: Unclear or constrained access to local data (e.g., electronic health record summaries and PRECISE-Value model inputs) limited the ability to include institution-specific evidence in the prototype.
justification: Data access requirements outside the design team prevented designers from integrating local evidence and analytic tools into the user flow, hindering the ability to specify requirements, produce more complete prototypes, and meaningfully evaluate designs with realistic data.
reference_excerpt: Feedback also indicated a need to improve our initial design so that the submissions made by stakeholders are more clearly summarized, and so that local evidence can be included in a report along with the stakeholder review summary. More work is needed to understand data access requirements to incorporate such a tool into the user process.

description: Maintaining accurate, up-to-date directory information about potential stakeholders (credentials, roles, prior engagement) is challenging because individuals change roles and affiliations.
justification: This external data-maintenance constraint limits the designers' ability to implement and validate the prototype's stakeholder search and selection functionality, hindering understanding of users and the ability to facilitate stakeholder involvement reliably.
reference_excerpt: Feasibility to provide the most accurate and up-to-date information in requested areas, however, requires further investigation. Individuals, for example, may change career roles, employment, expertise, and location which can create challenges to maintaining such up-to-date information.

description: A substantial portion of collected synthesized comments (39%, N=54) were not relevant to the study's focal design considerations, producing noisy or low-priority feedback.
justification: Irrelevant or off-target user feedback reduced the efficiency and focus of the team's analysis and slowed integration of actionable user input, hindering the integrate-feedback & iteration and evaluation workloads.
reference_excerpt: Second, many of the synthesized comments were not relevant to the design considerations of focus in this work (39%, N=54). Other synthesized comments will be used to identify lower-priority design improvements.

description: Many low-literacy patients refused to participate in tasks that required reading (including literacy tests), preventing direct measurement of literacy and forcing researchers to rely on a proxy measure.
justification: This interactional reluctance limited the team's ability to manage user understanding and to specify accurate user requirements based on measured literacy levels.
reference_excerpt: Many low-literacy patients refuse to participate in any study that requires reading (including taking a literacy test), because they lose standing with their peers. Thus, we used education levels as a proxy for literacy.

description: Difficulty obtaining actual consumption levels and incomplete recording by subjects meant researchers lacked reliable ground-truth data on what subjects actually consumed.
justification: Lack of accurate consumption measurements prevented the team from fully evaluating compliance and the effectiveness of the design, hindering the 'evaluate designs' and 'manage user understanding' workloads.
reference_excerpt: One limitation of the study was that given the difficulty in obtaining actual consumption levels, we do not know how compliant subjects were in monitoring. Interdialytic weight gain values do tell us subjects only recorded 56% of the fluid they consumed.

description: The barcode scanner technology (Socket SDIO In-Hand Scan Card) frequently failed: subjects could not successfully scan items the majority of attempts.
justification: High scanner failure rates limited the team's ability to evaluate and rely on scanning as an input mechanism, constraining user testing, iteration, and the specification of usable input methods.
reference_excerpt: Subjects could not successfully scan an item 87.9% of the time they attempted to do so. Only four subjects successfully scanned an item on their own.

description: Some subjects did not take the device outside the home or use it in front of strangers, indicating stigma or privacy concerns around using the PDA publicly.
justification: This user reluctance impeded the designers' ability to study context of use and to facilitate naturalistic user involvement and evaluation of the system outside the dialysis unit.
reference_excerpt: Some subjects did not take DIMA out of the home and/or did not use DIMA in front of strangers.

description: The PDA's limited screen size prevented displaying feedback for all monitored nutrients on every screen.
justification: This hardware constraint forced trade-offs in information presentation and hindered the designers' ability to address the holistic experience and fully specify feedback requirements.
reference_excerpt: DIMA could not include feedback for all six items on every screen because of the limited screen size. Instead, DIMA has a feedback bar at the bottom of the build-a-meal screen that provides the user with the ability to see their consumption levels for the most critical nutrients at a glance—fluid, sodium, and potassium.

description: Loss of devices during the study caused incomplete interaction logs for at least one subject.
justification: Data loss reduced the completeness of usage data, hindering evaluation of the design and interpretation of user behavior during iteration and assessment activities.
reference_excerpt: Unfortunately, subject 17 lost his PDA during the study, and so we only have a partially complete interaction log for that subject.

description: Socioeconomic costs (data plan expense) and privacy concerns among subjects limited options for synchronizing the app with remote records or using phone-based data plans.
justification: External cost and privacy constraints prevented designers from adopting certain technical implementations (eg, remote synchronization) and affected planning for future platform choices, constraining specification and operationalization of system features.
reference_excerpt: the necessary data plan is currently too costly for many subjects with low-socioeconomic status, and subjects may not want to share the information with providers.

description: Funding agency and IRB requirements constrained the number of planned design-and-test iterations, limiting flexibility to extend iterative cycles.
justification: External regulatory and funding constraints prevented designers from performing additional iteration and integrating further feedback, hindering the workload of integrating feedback & iteration and evaluating designs over extended cycles.
reference_excerpt: We planned the number of design-and-test iterations early in the project to satisfy the requirements of the funding agency and Institutional Review Board (IRB). As the project progressed, it became apparent that those assumptions were correct and that to adhere to budget and project timeline restrictions, we would be able to complete the 3 planned iterations.

description: Logistical burdens (meeting recruitment goals, preparing materials, coordinating geographically dispersed members) consumed resources and complicated UCD activities.
justification: These logistical constraints limited designers' ability to facilitate user involvement, manage user understanding (through timely data collection), and coordinate multidisciplinary team activities necessary for iterative design and evaluation.
reference_excerpt: Many of our recurring challenges were related to logistics, such as meeting recruitment goals, preparing and managing materials (ie, instructions, presentations, and design documentation), and arranging a specific time for members and advisors to meet despite being geographically dispersed.

description: Disciplinary diversity produced disagreement, communication difficulties, and differences in assumptions that were not automatically reconciled within the team.
justification: Cultural and methodological misalignment among team members hindered the workload of coordinating a multidisciplinary team and maintaining a shared understanding necessary for coherent design and iteration.
reference_excerpt: However, with disciplinary diversity comes disagreement, communication difficulty, and differences in assumptions, and although these are all desirable elements, they require efforts to manage, for example, by frequently asking team members to state their assumptions.

description: The volume and depth of formative interview data exceeded the team's analytic capacity within the available time, delaying discovery of important findings.
justification: Excess data that could not be analyzed in time prevented timely management of user understanding and integration of formative insights into design decisions and iteration.
reference_excerpt: The number and depth of P2P interviews yielded more data than could be analyzed in the time allotted. As a result, several important findings from stakeholder interviews were not discovered until further in the design process, negating some of the benefits of early learning.

description: Stakeholder samples were limited in diversity and representativeness (eg, patients were all white and predominantly male; advisors were more educated and engaged).
justification: Limited and unrepresentative stakeholder recruitment constrained designers' ability to manage user understanding and to specify requirements that reflect the broader target population.
reference_excerpt: The patients we interviewed in our formative research were all white, and two-third were male. Patient advisors were more likely to be educated and engaged in their health than peers, consistent with the general trend that patient advisors are rarely ordinary people.

description: Staff turnover and staffing limitations meant that only one design team member had participated in most formative activities and thus acted as the primary voice of patients.
justification: Loss of continuity and few team members with firsthand user exposure hindered designers' ability to manage user understanding, facilitate stakeholder involvement, and coordinate across phases of UCD.
reference_excerpt: One project member personally participated in almost every interview, feedback session, design meeting, and usability test. However, she was the only design team member who had interviewed patients and was therefore expected to be the voice of patient participants on the design team. Over time, turnover greatly reduced the number of team members who had been present from the beginning of the project and had therefore participated in any formative research activities.

description: Persistent designer assumptions and biases led to design choices that were not aligned with user preferences (for example, incorporating rewards that users found distracting).
justification: Cognitive and attitudinal biases prevented designers from accurately managing user understanding and from producing solutions that aligned with user needs, undermining evaluation and iteration workloads.
reference_excerpt: Designer bias is difficult to overcome, even when UCD methods are used to collect contradictory evidence. In the P2P project, for example, we incorporated rewards based on the literature. Nothing in the formative data contradicted the potential value of rewards, so it was not until testing that we learned that most participants thought the rewards were distracting.

description: Scope creep and excessive feature complexity led the team to design many features in parallel, reducing time and effort available for each feature's design and testing.
justification: Overly broad scope and complexity constrained designers' ability to specify clear requirements, produce focused design solutions, and perform sufficient evaluation and iteration on individual features.
reference_excerpt: As a result, we attempted to include in a single app a large variety of features. We also attempted to integrate these many features to produce a coherent product. Often, multiple features were being slowly designed in parallel, rather than perfecting 1 feature before moving on to the next. These conditions sometimes led to confusion about the purpose of the app. More features also meant less time and effort spent designing or testing each.

description: Tensions between designers, clinicians, and patients over innovation versus clinical reality led to disagreements about what features or information were appropriate or feasible.
justification: Divergent stakeholder knowledge, preferences, and clinical constraints impeded designers' ability to produce solutions that both innovated and fit clinical workflows, thus hindering specification of requirements and integration of stakeholder feedback.
reference_excerpt: In our experience, designers, clinician stakeholders, and patient stakeholders were divided on what was possible for and needed from the product being designed. Generally, clinicians were more conservative, preferring to replicate existing practices and avoid less studied or riskier options. For instance, clinicians were more conservative than designers about how much unedited information and control over its interpretation to offer patients.

description: Laboratory-based usability testing provided limited external validity and was easier to run, while in-the-wild testing was more valid but expensive and time-intensive, limiting field evaluation.
justification: Resource trade-offs between lab and field testing constrained designers' ability to evaluate designs in realistic contexts and to integrate longer-term use feedback into iterations.
reference_excerpt: P2P usability testing was conducted in a laboratory setting... this setting was more challenging because it required participants to test prototypes in a time and place dissimilar from the intended context of use. In-the-wild testing is expensive and time-intensive and may not be possible in every project.

description: Standardized evaluation methods required adaptation for older adults (eg, simplified SUS, accommodating breaks, handling vision and motor impairments), indicating limited fit of standard tools to the population.
justification: Lack of suitable, validated methods for the target population hindered designers' ability to evaluate designs reliably and to facilitate meaningful user involvement without compromising data quality.
reference_excerpt: We adapted the standard methods in several ways, including accommodating older adult participants. For example, we administered a simplified version of the System Usability Scale (SUS) self-report measure, which we developed specifically for older adults. We also discovered challenges that we had not anticipated, for example, a participant having difficulty completing computer-based surveys because of vision and motor impairment.

description: Using multiple concurrent evaluation methods increased session burden and data volume, sometimes causing sessions to be cut short and slowing analysis and iteration.
justification: High measurement and data-processing workload reduced the team's capacity to rapidly analyze findings and prepare subsequent prototypes, hindering the integrate feedback & iteration and evaluate designs workloads.
reference_excerpt: At times, the multiplicity of methods in a single session resulted in testing sessions being cut short. Moreover, the amount of data collected during testing affected the speed at which the team could analyze usability test findings and prepare the next design for another round of testing.

description: Time and budget constraints caused the team to avoid resource-intensive methods (field studies and interviews), limiting deep contextual user research.
justification: This resource limitation prevented designers from performing the 'understand context of use' and 'manage user understanding' workloads because they explicitly chose less time-consuming methods over in-depth user research.
reference_excerpt: Thus, being associated to the time and budget allotted for the project, demotivating factors [30] and knowing restrictions, the most relevant methods, "Field studies" and "Interviews with users" require a long time for its implementation and commonly greater investment [31], we opted to choose methods to balance these two factors.

description: Differences in attitudes among multidisciplinary team members and communication failures created weaknesses during development.
justification: Interpersonal and attitudinal issues disrupted coordination of the multidisciplinary team and hindered collaboration needed to integrate feedback, iterate, and maintain shared user understanding.
reference_excerpt: In this line, it is considered that the diversity of skills/roles of the various elements of the multidisciplinary team may also have created weaknesses throughout the development process. These difficulties have focused primarily at the level of the difference in attitudes of the team members, as well as communication failures.

description: Conflicting expectations between the commissioning company (seeking reduced costs) and external developers (seeking to maximize collaboration) created misaligned incentives.
justification: These stakeholder-driven cost and scope pressures constrained designers' ability to balance product quality, design time, and development costs, thereby limiting iteration, holistic experience work, and producing optimal design solutions.
reference_excerpt: Working in multidisciplinary teams can create different involvements. For example, the company that developed the Courseware Sere, the Ludomedia, you want it to have reduced development costs. On the other hand, an external developer might want to make the most of their collaboration.

description: There was no designated 'facilitator of User Centered Design' within the team to mediate between users and technical members.
justification: The absence of a dedicated facilitator limited the team's capacity to coordinate user involvement, ensure user perspectives were integrated across disciplines, and sustain iterative evaluation and feedback loops.
reference_excerpt: In an upcoming project, an important factor would be to ensure that as one of the team members, were given the responsibility/role of "facilitator of User Centered Design" in the development process. The facilitator of User Centered Design mediates the relationship between users and the elements of the multidisciplinary team and should have a multidisciplinary background (for example, see how users interact with educational software and understand the context of use) [20].

description: The COVID-19 pandemic prevented safe in-person engagement, forcing the team to shift to web-based methods that change access and participation dynamics.
justification: This external constraint limited the team's ability to conduct in-person user research and contextual inquiry, hindering their ability to understand context of use and to facilitate certain types of user involvement and iterative design activities.
reference_excerpt: Moreover, the COVID-19 pandemic hindered our ability to engage safely with participants, and these web-based methods enable our research to continue despite current limitations on in-person research activities.

description: Eligibility required participants to have internet, video camera, audio, and microphone access, excluding youth without these resources.
justification: Requiring specific technology prevented the researchers from recruiting and involving SGMY without adequate devices or connectivity, limiting participant diversity and constraining the team’s ability to manage user understanding and study contexts of use.
reference_excerpt: Eligible youth are aged 14 years to 18 years, live in the United States, identify as sexual and/or gender minorities, and have internet, video camera, audio, and microphone access to attend the virtual sessions.

description: All sessions were conducted in English, excluding non-English-speaking SGMY from participation.
justification: Limiting sessions to English reduced the researchers' ability to engage a linguistically diverse sample, which constrains understanding of varied user experiences and limits facilitation of inclusive user involvement and holistic experience design.
reference_excerpt: All the sessions will be conducted in English.

description: Recruitment fell short of the planned sample: far fewer participants consented and attended than the target 45-60.
justification: The lower-than-planned enrollment and attendance limited the researchers' capacity to generate the intended breadth of ideas and to sustain iterative activities and evaluation across cohorts, hindering facilitate user involvement and produce/evaluate design solutions.
reference_excerpt: A total of 50 participants were invited to participate, and 22 consented to participate. In total, 16 SGMY participated in at least one human-centered design session.

description: The team intentionally did not ask participants about their personal experiences with adolescent relationship abuse to avoid harm.
justification: This ethical decision constrained the depth of first-person experiential data the researchers could collect, limiting their ability to manage deep user understanding and specify rich user requirements for intervention design.
reference_excerpt: It is important to note that we never inquired about participants’personal experiences with ARA.

description: The study excluded other stakeholder groups (eg, parents and school personnel) from participation.
justification: Omitting additional relevant stakeholders limited designers' ability to address the holistic experience and contextual determinants of interventions, reducing perspectives available to inform requirements and concept development.
reference_excerpt: In addition to youth, the inclusion of other stakeholders (eg, parents and school personnel) would likely have important insights for intervention concepts, but they are not included in this study.

description: The 30-day challenge format (rigid, day-by-day delivery with fixed order and no skipping) failed to engage junior physicians in practice, leading to early discontinuation of use.
justification: This interactional problem limited designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and to evaluate and iterate on content because users disengaged quickly, reducing opportunities for meaningful feedback and testing of the intended delivery model.
reference_excerpt: Inspection of app use data revealed that discontinuation of the 30-day challenge tended to appear around day 5... With the 30-day challenge format, users were unable to skip challenge topics or change the order of challenges, possibly facilitating the discontinuation of app use.

description: Junior physicians were time-poor and perceived the app as 'another chore' amid long working hours, which reduced their willingness to engage with the prototype.
justification: Users' limited time availability is an environmental/resource constraint that hindered designers' ability to facilitate user involvement, understand real-world use patterns, and obtain sufficient engagement data for iteration and evaluation.
reference_excerpt: The main app use barrier reported by the participants was that the app would feel like another chore when participants were already time-poor and working long hours.

description: Informational sessions were underutilized, possibly because they had less-prominent positioning within the app, reducing exposure and uptake of those contents.
justification: This design/positioning issue impeded designers' ability to address the holistic experience and to evaluate the usefulness of informational content, limiting their capacity to refine content placement and access based on user behavior.
reference_excerpt: In addition, informational sessions were underutilized in comparison to challenge content, possibly due to their less-prominent positioning within the app.

description: The team initially planned to adapt the evidence-based HeadGear 30-day challenge format for junior physicians, but modifying a delivery format from one population to another proved not always successful.
justification: This planning-level assumption about transferability constrained designers' ability to specify appropriate user requirements and produce effective design solutions for the new population, necessitating substantial redesign after pilot data showed poor engagement.
reference_excerpt: Hence, one option available to our team was to utilize the 30-day challenge format of the evidence-based HeadGear app and to modify the clinical content to meet the needs of junior physicians... simply modifying the modes of content delivery (ie, 30-day challenge structure) from one evidence-based app to suit another working population is not always successful.

description: Participant recruitment relied on convenience and snowball sampling within the authors' networks, limiting diversity and the team's ability to generalize findings or capture varied user contexts.
justification: This sampling constraint reduced the designers' ability to manage user understanding and to understand contexts of use broadly, constraining specification of user requirements and reducing confidence in evaluation results' generalizability.
reference_excerpt: our participants were identified through convenience and snowball sampling within the authors’ networks, and thus are likely to be more experienced with the clinical application of microbial genomics.

description: The team lacked a priori knowledge of effect sizes for their design-choice questions, making formal sample size calculations impractical.
justification: This methodological uncertainty hindered the designers' capacity to plan rigorous evaluation (Evaluate designs) and to power quantitative comparisons, limiting the strength of inferences drawn from participant preference data.
reference_excerpt: we did not have a priori knowledge of the effect sizes (i.e., extent of preferential difference for each type of question) in the Design Choice Questionnaire, making sample size calculations challenging.

description: Stakeholders reported that laboratory reports are delivered via diverse media (PDFs in EHRs, faxes, physical mail), requiring the redesigned report to be legible in black-and-white and ruling out interactive or color-dependent designs.
justification: These external delivery and format constraints limited the designers' ability to produce certain design solutions (Produce design solutions) and constrained choices around interactivity and use of color, affecting how the team structured and emphasized information.
reference_excerpt: experts indicated that laboratory reports were delivered using a variety of formats, including PDFs appended to electronic health records, faxes, or physical mail. This created design constraints at the outset of the project—our redesigned report needed to be legible no matter the medium, ruling out online interactivity, and needed to be black and white.

description: Many participants reported low confidence interpreting several WGS-related data types, indicating limited user familiarity with genomic outputs.
justification: Users' limited domain knowledge constrained designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and to rely on participants for valid evaluation feedback (Manage user understanding; Evaluate designs), requiring the team to adapt designs and add educational/interpretive elements.
reference_excerpt: most participants only felt somewhat confident, or not confident at all, interpreting the other data types (Table S3).

description: Clinicians and non-clinicians disagreed on the level of detail and types of genomic information to include, producing divergent preferences for report content and presentation.
justification: Conflicting stakeholder preferences impeded integration of feedback and iteration as designers had to reconcile opposing needs (Integrate feedback & iteration; Specify user requirements), ultimately defaulting to clinician preferences in some cases.
reference_excerpt: experts had differing perceptions of data types and desired level of detail between clinicians and non-clinicians, perhaps reflecting the clinicians’ procedural need for rapid interpretation.

description: Key external data resources were unavailable or difficult to obtain (e.g., prior patient test results; final mutation catalog), preventing inclusion or testing of certain design elements.
justification: Limited access to upstream data sources constrained the designers' ability to specify requirements and to evaluate representations that depended on those data (Understand context of use; Evaluate designs), delaying or preventing testing of some elements.
reference_excerpt: prior test results from a patient were deemed important; however, the earlier expert consults indicated that such data was difficult to obtain and unlikely to be included in future reports. ... we did not test any design elements displaying the strength of the association between the mutation and the resistance phenotype; however, we will add this to a future version of the report pending receipt of the final mutation catalog from the ReSeqTB Consortium.

description: Technical limitations of downstream systems (EHRs, photocopying) threatened the fidelity of emphasis features (bolding/shading), constraining how emphasis could be used in designs.
justification: Concerns that emphasis styling might not transfer correctly limited designers' choices for information emphasis, affecting Produce design solutions and Evaluate designs across real-world media.
reference_excerpt: some reported concerns as to whether such emphasis was possible with current electronic health records, including "[bolding or shading] may not transfer correctly" and "shaded [text] won’t photocopy well."

description: Caregivers were too overwhelmed to participate in usability testing, so the team recruited healthy older adults instead of target caregivers.
justification: Limited access to target users constrained the designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and to develop deep, context-rich understanding of actual caregiver needs for evaluation and iteration.
reference_excerpt: As a consequence, we decided to privilege the recruitment of a group of healthy older persons rather than the (overwhelmed) caregivers for usability tests.

description: Planned interactive features (contact a professional and videoconferencing) were not implemented due to lack of resources.
justification: Resource scarcity prevented the team from producing and integrating these design solutions, limiting the holistic experience and reducing the scope of feature iteration.
reference_excerpt: Unfortunately the option “contact a professional” and the videoconferencing options were not implemented, owing to a lack of resources.

description: A private diary feature ('My journey') was removed because the system could not encrypt the data.
justification: A technical/security limitation stopped designers from implementing a user-requested feature, hindering the production of privacy-sensitive design solutions and the integration of user feedback.
reference_excerpt: Moreover, the section “My journey”, a private diary for caregivers, was removed because the system could not encrypt the data.

description: Several usability problems (forum/video-player font size, forum post button position, double-click conflict with light box) remained unsolved due to technical or logistical reasons.
justification: Unresolved technical/logistical constraints limited the team's ability to iterate and fully address identified usability issues, impairing evaluation and integration of user feedback into subsequent designs.
reference_excerpt: Some other issues remained unsolved due to technical or logistical reasons: (1) the font size and symbols in the forum and video-player interfaces did not facilitate reading; (2) the post button for forum messages was at the bottom of the screen, requiring the use of the scrollbar; and (3) the least experienced participants often double clicked in the website, which was in conflict with the one-click activated “light box” effect, as the second click immediately closed the window.

description: Website rendering varied across Internet browsers and computer models, creating inconsistent displays during testing.
justification: Environmental variability hindered accurate evaluation and understanding of the context of use, forcing designers to adapt documentation rather than resolving root compatibility issues.
reference_excerpt: The website display varied according to the Internet browser and/or the computer model, and some participants did not know how to use the hyperlinks in the website.

description: Participants conflated the website interface with the Internet browser and operating system (eg, invisible cursor/scrollbar, closing browser instead of navigating), complicating usability interpretation.
justification: This interactional and environmental confusion impeded designers' ability to disentangle website-specific problems from broader system issues, limiting accurate user understanding and evaluation of the site itself.
reference_excerpt: The mouse cursor and the scrollbar were not visible enough on the screen (lack of contrast or small size), and some participants did not distinguish the website settings from the Internet browser or computer interface. For instance, a participant recommended changing the order of icons of the Internet browser because he thought that the latter was part of the website. When asked to go back to the “home page” of the website, another participant closed the browser window, then could not find, unaided, the icon of the Internet browser to continue the task.

description: Their usability questionnaire lacked items to measure 'learnability' and 'usefulness,' and no field pilot tests were performed during development.
justification: This methodological gap limited the team's ability to evaluate and measure important dimensions of user learning and real-world usefulness, constraining evaluation activities and the ability to plan iterative improvements.
reference_excerpt: First, even if our usability questionnaire was more adapted to our project context, it did not include items intended to measure “learnability” and “usefulness” perceptions, instead, we conducted the interviews at the end of the evaluations exploring these constructs. To improve the analysis of both dimensions, we recommend to conduct a field study during the development process, such as pilot tests in which the users have access to the program for one or two weeks.

description: The team lacked ergonomics expertise early in development and relied on open-source 'ready-to-use' programs that did not meet universal design criteria.
justification: Insufficient ergonomic skill and choice of unsuitable third-party components prevented the prevention of early ergonomic mistakes, hindering the ability to address holistic experience and produce accessible design solutions.
reference_excerpt: we think that some ergonomic mistakes in the first versions of our website could have been prevented earlier in the development process, with the help of an expert in ergonomics at these stages. For instance, we recommend avoiding the use of open source “ready-to-use” programs, since they do not always respond to the universal design criteria.

description: The study had a relatively small sample size and was conducted in a limited Western, densely populated context, restricting the breadth of user evidence available to the research team.
justification: This resource limitation constrained the designers' ability to manage user understanding and to understand varied contexts of use, reducing confidence in requirements and limiting evaluation generalisability for iterative design work.
reference_excerpt: In terms of limitations, the work reflects a relatively small sample size and limited context – therefore results should be interpreted on the basis of a Western context and densely populated region with good public infrastructure.

description: Wide variation in participants' technology literacy and unequal access to personal technology complicated participant engagement and the representativeness of feedback.
justification: Differences in technology familiarity and access hindered facilitation of user involvement and the team's ability to specify consistent user requirements and evaluate prototypes across the target population.
reference_excerpt: Amongst the small group, there was a wide spread in terms of technology literacy – all owned a smartphone – yet some participants were more comfortable with technology than others.

description: Qualitative coding was initially carried out by a single author before group refinement, creating a risk of individual bias in analysis.
justification: Relying on one analyst initially could limit the designers' ability to accurately manage user understanding and integrate feedback into iterative design decisions, affecting the validity of thematic findings used to drive requirements and prototypes.
reference_excerpt: In line with Braun and Clarke’s original interpretation, the coding process was initially carried out by solely the first author13 [8, 9, 74]. Following this, all the authors met and collectively refined and discussed the themes together to mitigate individual bias.

description: User-testing and iterative feedback for prototypes were conducted with small, limited specialist groups (e.g., only two SLTs for one prototype and five specialists for another).
justification: These small testing rounds constrained the team's capacity to thoroughly evaluate designs and iterate based on diverse user and stakeholder feedback, limiting confidence in design refinements and broader applicability.
reference_excerpt: a final version of the prototype underwent a small round of user-testing with the two SLTs ... the prototype was iterated on the basis of further suggestions and feedback from user-testing of the prototype with 5 specialists from the centre.

description: Designers were unable to test interactive navigation of the GMA because task walkthroughs did not involve a working prototype, limiting hands-on usability evaluation.
justification: This resource limitation prevented designers from performing evaluation workloads (testing interactive prototypes with users) and constrained their ability to integrate feedback and iterate based on actual user interactions.
reference_excerpt: While actual navigation of the GMA software interface could not be tested during our task walkthroughs, participants still proposed several areas to improve (Table 5).

description: Broader system and organizational constraints (laboratory–EHR communication and incorrect notification of care team members) could not be solved within the project scope, limiting design solutions.
justification: These external system and scope constraints hindered designers' ability to understand the full context of use and to specify actionable requirements or implement design changes that would address end-to-end workflows.
reference_excerpt: Some challenges brought up in phase 1 focus groups could not be addressed directly in the design of the GMA. For example, a clear need identified by participants was to improve the communication between laboratory systems and the EHR. Focus group participants also reported that some processes for notifying clinicians of genetic test results do not notify the correct members of the care team in the TPP project. In both instances, solutions for these needs were beyond the scope of this project.

description: The study focused on single-point delivery scenarios and did not explore mechanisms for updating interpretations over time, limiting consideration of longitudinal reporting needs.
justification: This scope/resource limitation prevented designers from addressing holistic experience and requirements related to evolving genetic information, constraining their ability to design notification and update workflows and to manage user understanding over time.
reference_excerpt: The scenarios we present in this work, however, were for the delivery of results at one point in time, and do not explore potential changes to interpretations over time. Complementing that work would be research to better understand approaches to notify clinicians of updates to GS findings and interpretations.

description: Resource constraints and a small sample size prevented completion of later UCD stages and limited the study's ability to move beyond medium-fidelity testing.
justification: The lack of budget and human resources halted the Implementation Phase and restricted further iterations and higher-fidelity evaluation, directly hindering evaluation of designs and integration of feedback/iteration workloads.
reference_excerpt: Due to resource constraints, the study's sample size is small and insufficient to illustrate the presence or absence of causal relationships on explored variables. The Implementation Phase of the UCD methodology was not done.

description: Participant attrition (three health workers resigned) reduced continuity of user involvement and altered the respondent pool during the two-month UCD process.
justification: Loss of participants during the study constrained the team's ability to maintain ongoing user involvement and manage evolving user understanding across iterative design activities.
reference_excerpt: (Three of these 30 health workers dropped out of the two-month long UCD process when they resigned from the RHU within the duration of this study. Hence, the change of 'respondents' data reported for subsequent questions.)

description: On-site or regional training events were costly and staff turnover meant that training benefits left with departing HCWs, limiting sustainable user competence.
justification: High cost of in-person training and turnover prevented reliable cascading of knowledge, constraining the designers' ability to facilitate user involvement, sustain training, and ensure long-term usability in the field.
reference_excerpt: On-site or regional training events are costly and require the HCW to leave the RHU for a certain period, which in turn slows down health care services. Moreover, when HCWs trained on the technology leave the RHU, the knowledge leaves with them.

description: A requested search function in the medium-fidelity prototype existed only as a non-functional placeholder, preventing full user testing of that feature.
justification: Because the search button was not implemented, designers could not fully evaluate or iterate that functionality with users, limiting the evaluate designs and integrate feedback workloads.
reference_excerpt: The users greatly appreciated the search button. They specifically requested this function when the Low Fidelity Prototype was being discussed. In the medium fidelity prototype design phase, the search buttons were just placeholders and not yet functional.

description: Many RHU staff were described as not open to learning complicated things and were often afraid to handle a device, reflecting resistance and low confidence among users.
justification: These attitudes and fears reduced designers' ability to engage users comfortably, complicating management of user understanding and facilitation of involvement required for iterative testing and requirement elicitation.
reference_excerpt: It was also observed that RHU staff are no longer open to learning complicated things or are often afraid to handle a device.

description: Physicians and some provider professions were under-represented in the sample, likely because busy clinical schedules reduced engagement in voluntary research.
justification: This recruitment bias limited the researchers' ability to manage comprehensive user understanding and to facilitate involvement from all relevant provider types, constraining the representativeness of feedback used to specify requirements and plan implementation.
reference_excerpt: Nearly 40% of the sample were psychologists, and as such other professions may be under represented in the current study, possibly due to that physicians busy schedules may reduce engagement in voluntary research studies.

description: Participants only received the draft RISE manual to review if they had time and were given up to 20 minutes during the interview to review it.
justification: Constrained participant preparation time impeded the researchers' ability to elicit deep, informed feedback and to evaluate the intervention thoroughly, limiting the quality of user understanding and design evaluation.
reference_excerpt: Prior to the interview, participants received the draft RISE manual to review if time permitted.

description: Undue influences such as social desirability may have affected provider responses to study team members.
justification: Social desirability and related interpersonal response biases hindered researchers' ability to obtain candid user feedback, reducing the validity of insights used to integrate feedback and iterate on the design.
reference_excerpt: Additionally, it is possible that other undue influences (e.g., social desirability) may have impacted provider response to study team members about the RISE intervention.

description: The study did not formally assess providers' level of training or experience with IPV.
justification: Omitting measurement of provider IPV experience reduced the researchers' ability to characterize user subgroups and to translate nuanced user knowledge into precise requirements and targeted training design.
reference_excerpt: Further, the current study did not formerly assess for provider’s level of training in or experience with IPV, which may have influenced results.

description: Data collection was limited to two VHA medical centers in the New England region, constraining regional and system diversity of informants.
justification: Restricted geographic/site scope limited researchers' ability to understand broader contexts of use and to generalize findings across varied implementation settings, impeding context-driven design decisions.
reference_excerpt: Providers interviewed in this study work at VA Healthcare Systems in the New England region of the US, and therefore findings may be specific to these regions and healthcare systems.

description: Some participants reported that IPV interventions were not perceived as a priority by clinics, the healthcare system, or leadership.
justification: Organizational lack of prioritization by external stakeholders constrained researchers' ability to plan feasible implementation strategies, to facilitate provider involvement, and to secure support needed for iterative testing in routine care.
reference_excerpt: Some participants expressed that an IPV intervention was not perceived as a priority by the clinic, the healthcare system, and/or the leadership.

description: Providers identified limited time, resources, and physical space in primary care and other busy clinical settings as barriers to delivering RISE.
justification: Clinical workload and setting constraints hindered the researchers' ability to evaluate and iterate the intervention in fast-paced primary care contexts and impeded eliciting realistic implementation feasibility data from users.
reference_excerpt: Participants identified several potential barriers to implementing RISE. Participants also identified barriers such as the limited time, resources, and space available in primary care and other busy clinical settings.

description: Severe time and budget constraints (8 weeks and €2000) limited the team's ability to run further iterations, conduct additional user-testing cycles, and outsource specialist expertise.
justification: These resource limits constrained the team's ability to integrate feedback and iterate further, produce higher-fidelity design solutions, and evaluate alternative prototypes with broader samples.
reference_excerpt: Resource-use for the project was minimal, as this was conducted over 8 weeks as an undergraduate summer student project supported by Evidence Synthesis Ireland for €2000. ... our limited time and resources hindered our ability to outsource expertise (e.g., the hiring of a digital media company ...).

description: Time restraints led the team to have researchers, rather than members of the public, determine the initial key messages, making the approach not fully user-centred.
justification: This decision limited the team's ability to manage user understanding from the outset and to facilitate early user involvement in specifying requirements, constraining downstream iteration and alignment with public perspectives.
reference_excerpt: However, our use of researchers to determine the initial key messages of the resource meant that our approach was not fully 'user-centred'. Given ... our time restraints, we felt it a necessary pragmatic starting point for those identifying the initial key messages to have a solid understanding of evidence synthesis.

description: Use of convenience sampling resulted in some public participants being known to lead authors and possibly feeling pressure not to be critical, reducing candour of feedback.
justification: This interactional pressure impeded honest user involvement and the validity of evaluative feedback, thereby weakening designers' ability to accurately understand users and integrate authentic critiques into iteration.
reference_excerpt: A limitation of our approach is the use of convenience sampling. This meant that some of the members of the public involved were known to the lead authors (CD and ET), and therefore may have felt some degree of pressure not to be too critical of the resource for fear of offending.

description: A short recruitment timeframe and difficulties recruiting minors (due to requirement for parent/guardian consent) reduced the diversity and completeness of the participant sample.
justification: Limited recruitment time and barriers to enrolling minors constrained the team's ability to facilitate broad user involvement and to manage a deep, representative understanding of users across age groups and contexts of use.
reference_excerpt: The timeframe of the recruitment for participants was one week. ... we were successful in recruiting one male and female participant from each age category except in the <18 years category where one male was recruited, due to the fact that minors are more difficult to recruit given the necessity of parent/guardian consent.

description: There is limited evidence-based guidance on optimal video duration for educational KT resources, creating uncertainty for designers when specifying length requirements.
justification: This knowledge gap constrained the team's ability to define and justify specific user requirements (optimal duration) and to evaluate trade-offs between brevity and comprehensiveness during design decisions.
reference_excerpt: There is limited evidence-based definitive guidance on determining the optimal duration of videos such as ours, with much variability reported in the literature. ... We aimed to keep our video as brief as possible with an absolute cut-off of 4 min, and frequently revisited the issue of length with all stakeholders involved.

description: Many recruited clients did not attend confirmed design sessions, reducing participant numbers available for co-design and usability testing. This diminished end-user involvement constrained iterative design activities.
justification: Participants' nonattendance directly hindered the designers' ability to facilitate user involvement, manage evolving user understanding, and run sufficient evaluation and iteration cycles (phases 2–4).
reference_excerpt: We intended to recruit 8 clients and members of their social networks in design rounds 2, 4, and 5. Approximately half of the recruited participants (n=9) did not show up at these design rounds (phases 2 and 3).

description: Designers were unable to recruit as many members of clients' social networks as intended, resulting in limited participation from this stakeholder group. This reduced diversity of input impeded exploration of social-network–related requirements and features.
justification: The limited involvement of social network members constrained designers' ability to understand those actors' contexts and needs, specify comprehensive user requirements, and iterate solutions addressing peer-related functionality.
reference_excerpt: Another limitation was the involvement of a limited number of members of women’s social networks in most rounds of intervention design. Identical to clients' no shows, we were not able to recruit as many members of social networks as intended.

description: The target population for recruitment was very small (fewer than 1% of births qualify for the program), limiting the available pool of end users for design activities. This made recruiting sufficient participants for iterative rounds challenging.
justification: A small eligible population reduced designers' capacity to manage user understanding and facilitate user involvement across multiple iterative sessions, constraining the robustness and generalizability of requirements gathering and testing.
reference_excerpt: Involving disadvantaged populations in research is challenging [5,53]. Moreover, with less than 1% of the births per Dutch municipality qualifying to enroll in VoorZorg, our target population is very small.

description: The prototype used for usability testing had limited functionality, which may have prevented detection of usability problems that would appear during free use. This limited maturity constrained the depth of evaluation possible in phase 4.
justification: Evaluating an early, functionally limited prototype restricted designers' ability to fully evaluate designs and integrate feedback from real-world use, thereby limiting iteration and refinement based on comprehensive usability insights.
reference_excerpt: Moreover, we evaluated the usability of a prototype with limited functionality. The think aloud method was based on certain real-life tasks that covered all the functionalities. This may have highlighted other usability problems that would have occurred during free use of the app. The limited functionality of the prototype may also have resulted in an incomplete insight into usability problems.

description: Usability testing revealed that users were unfamiliar with underlying source documentation that populated the tab, which confused users during evaluation tasks.
justification: This user knowledge gap limited the designers' ability to evaluate the tab accurately and gather valid usability feedback, hindering the 'evaluate designs' and 'manage user understanding' workloads.
reference_excerpt: This process revealed a lack of familiarity among users with some of the underlying documentation that sourced the data displayed in the tab.

description: Clinicians reported perceived lack of time, competing priorities, and difficulty remembering to launch the tab, reducing real-world engagement.
justification: Low clinician time and competing workflow priorities constrained designers' ability to facilitate user involvement, collect representative feedback, and run iterative evaluations in clinical settings.
reference_excerpt: Our early pilot data have also revealed potential barriers to large-scale implementation, which include perceived lack of time to engage with the tab, competing priorities, incomplete or inaccurate tab content, technical glitches, and difficulty remembering to launch the tab as part of routine workflow.

description: Technical performance issues (delays in displaying tab content and other glitches) required coordination with the information systems team to diagnose and fix.
justification: System performance problems impeded designers' ability to ensure usability and to evaluate the tab reliably, blocking evaluation and iteration until technical optimizations were made.
reference_excerpt: In addition, to detect delays in displaying information to the user that might decrease usability, we assessed the time to launch the tab content for selected patients. If time delays were identified, we worked with the information systems team to identify the source of the delay so that it could be rectified; specifically, technical optimizations were made to bring the load times in line with other feature load times in our EHR (ie, no longer than a few seconds).

description: The decision to make the tab read-only (with data editable only in source documents) constrained how the tab could be used and updated.
justification: This stakeholder-driven design constraint limited the designers' ability to facilitate direct user updates and rapid iterative edits within the tab, affecting 'facilitate user involvement' and 'integrate feedback & iteration' workloads.
reference_excerpt: The Patient Values Tab will be in a read-only format (ie, the data displayed will be captured and edited elsewhere). We chose this approach because we and various key stakeholders we interviewed were concerned that the content would become unwieldy and unstable, ultimately leading to inefficiency for users if multiple modifications were allowed.

description: Incomplete or inaccurate content in source documentation led to concerns about the tab's content quality.
justification: Poor or inconsistent upstream documentation limited designers' ability to ensure accurate information in the tab, hindering 'manage user understanding', 'specify user requirements', and 'evaluate designs' because the artifact's fidelity depended on external data quality.
reference_excerpt: Our early pilot data have also revealed potential barriers to large-scale implementation, which include perceived lack of time to engage with the tab, competing priorities, incomplete or inaccurate tab content, technical glitches, and difficulty remembering to launch the tab as part of routine workflow.

description: User testing revealed that some images took excessive time to identify, forcing the team to run an additional intermediate study to classify image difficulty levels, adding unplanned workload and time to the development process.
justification: Requiring an extra empirical study constrained the team's ability to iteratively refine content and slowed integration of user feedback, hindering the workloads of integrate feedback & iteration, evaluate designs, and produce design solutions (content).
reference_excerpt: it was observed that the user required an excessive amount of time to identify certain images, which made us consider the need to classify such content by difficulty levels and, therefore, to include an intermediate study in the development process, which is detailed below.

description: A subset of images could not be unambiguously assigned to a difficulty level using the chosen quantitative criteria, so researchers resorted to consensual, subjective allocation rather than objective methods.
justification: Lack of objective classification metrics or tools limited the team's ability to specify clear content requirements and produce reproducible design decisions for the image set, hindering the workloads of specify user requirements and produce design solutions (content classification).
reference_excerpt: A small number of the images generated and analyzed did not meet the two criteria of a certain level; that is, by LFJT Accuracy they belong to one level, and by mean RT they belong to the other. After conducting a subsequent study of the characteristics of the images of each level, the researchers decided, after some consensual rounds ... their ultimate allocation to their corresponding level.

description: General practitioners (GPs) were not involved in the early context-of-use and user-requirements analysis nor the first usability pilot, limiting designers' access to a key stakeholder group.
justification: GP nonparticipation reduced the design team's ability to manage user understanding and facilitate user involvement for a multidisciplinary system, constraining requirement specification and early evaluation activities.
reference_excerpt: In this study, the GPs, one group of users, are not involved in the context of use and user requirements analysis and the first usability evaluation pilot.

description: Home care nurses did not perform the intended daily triage because of workload and unfamiliarity with the task, leading them to share triage responsibilities.
justification: Nurses' limited capacity and need to adapt prevented designers from observing and evaluating the intended workflow, hindering understanding of the real context of use and integration of feedback into design iterations.
reference_excerpt: Home care nurses indicated that the daily triage of the report problems was necessary but not performed as intended because of workload and because they needed to get used to the daily task. Therefore, some home care nurses decided to share the triage task with nurses who had the capability to perform a triage.

description: The monitoring system lacked integration with electronic patient files, making adding new client profiles time-consuming and dependent on manual entry.
justification: Absence of EHR integration (an external technical/organizational constraint) limited designers' ability to evaluate real-world workflows and specify usable requirements for data entry and patient-management tasks.
reference_excerpt: Adding new client profiles in the monitoring and consulting webpage was experienced as time-consuming. ... Home care workers mentioned that a link between the electronic patient file and the monitoring and consulting webpage is desirable and will ensure that data of clients who are added to the home care will be automatically added to the monitoring and consulting webpage.

description: Feedback from GPs and pharmacists was relayed to home health care assistants by telephone rather than directly through the system, which was experienced as time-consuming.
justification: This communication workaround hindered designers' ability to evaluate and support integrated multidisciplinary feedback flows and constrained iterative improvements to in-system feedback mechanisms.
reference_excerpt: Home care nurses informed home health care assistants about the feedback of a GP or pharmacist by a telephone call, which was experienced as time consuming. The solution to forward feedback of a home care nurse, a GP, or a pharmacist from the monitoring and consulting webpage to the report webpage was mentioned.

description: The team used a low-fidelity prototype that was not fully functional, which prevented collecting feedback on performance and functionality.
justification: This methodological/resource limitation directly hindered the designers' ability to evaluate the prototype's runtime behavior and functionality with users, constraining the 'Evaluate designs' and 'Integrate feedback & iteration' workloads.
reference_excerpt: We did not collect feedback about the performance and the functionality as the application was a low-fidelity prototype.

description: Handling patients' data raises security and privacy challenges that must be resolved before deployment or field evaluation.
justification: These legal/organizational constraints limit the designers' ability to deploy and test the system in real clinical contexts and to use real patient data, impeding 'Evaluate designs', 'Produce design solutions', and iterative refinement based on live use.
reference_excerpt: Firstly, handling patients’ data involves security and privacy challenges that must be met with appropriate techniques and policies.

description: Access to external proprietary systems (medical databases and patient information systems) is administratively and technically challenging.
justification: These administrative and technical barriers prevent designers from integrating required data sources and implementing requested features, hindering 'Specify user requirements', 'Produce design solutions', and realistic 'Evaluate designs' in context.
reference_excerpt: Secondly, CANA should be able to communicate with various proprietary, subscription-based systems such as medical databases and patient information systems. Thus, administrative and technical challenges related to gaining access to external systems must be solved in order to implement all requested features.

description: The regional Apotti programme's current architecture does not mention mobile or context-aware services, limiting integration opportunities.
justification: Because the planned regional system lacks mobile/context-aware interfaces, designers cannot rely on unified integrated tools or data sources, constraining their ability to 'Understand context of use' across locations and to 'Produce design solutions' that leverage centralized data.
reference_excerpt: The current design of the architecture does not mention mobile or context-aware services.

description: Urgent timeline and need for same-day visualizations forced a lightweight user-centered design approach rather than a rigorous UCD process.
justification: Time pressure prevented thorough user research, deeper iteration cycles, and rigorous synthesis, hindering management of user understanding, facilitation of user involvement, and integration of feedback and iteration.
reference_excerpt: Because of the urgent need for visualizations, a rapid process of development and user feedback from domain experts and/or end users was developed. A rigorous user-centered design approach is not possible when the goal is to produce same day data visualizations.

description: Poor vendor interoperability and lack of standard APIs/data formats required manual and semi-automated data extraction with ongoing quality issues.
justification: Unreliable and heterogeneous data feeds constrained designers' ability to understand the context of use, produce accurate dashboards, stabilize metrics, and perform iterative evaluation and refinement.
reference_excerpt: As neither vendor fully supported industry-standard application programming interfaces nor a common data format, data were retrieved from their proprietary data platforms using semi-automated scripts and ingested into structured relational database tables. We also faced several challenges, including interoperability, poor vendor data standards, and challenges accessing real-time data.

description: No formal interrater reliability was used when synthesizing interview content, indicating a methodological rigor gap in qualitative synthesis.
justification: This lack of methodological rigor likely reduced consistency and trustworthiness of user insights, hindering the team's ability to manage user understanding and reliably specify user requirements.
reference_excerpt: Limitations to our approach include: no formal interrater reliability when synthesizing interview content, no design for different devices (eg, mobile phones, tablets, etc), and no consideration for users with disabilities.

description: Dashboards were not designed for different devices or for users with disabilities, and were not distributed to frontline clinical staff.
justification: Omitting device-specific designs, accessibility considerations, and frontline clinical users prevented addressing the holistic experience and limited facilitation of broader user involvement and requirement specification for those audiences.
reference_excerpt: Limitations to our approach include: no formal interrater reliability when synthesizing interview content, no design for different devices (eg, mobile phones, tablets, etc), and no consideration for users with disabilities. These dashboards were not distributed to frontline clinical staff.

description: The store-provided product database was incomplete, inconsistently labelled, and costly to revise, limiting the design team's ability to ensure accurate search results.
justification: Missing and mislabeled articles in the database prevented designers from achieving higher effectiveness in the search engine and constrained iterative usability improvements and valid evaluation of the interface.
reference_excerpt: This database consists of more than 60,000 different products, sometimes with several variations... Many terms and definitions did not conform with everyday language use. Further, not every article was included with its actual location.

description: The mobile robot was often unavailable for user testing because of intensive technical system revisions, forcing evaluations to be run on a stationary terminal instead.
justification: Lack of access to the mobile robot impeded designers' ability to evaluate and iterate the full embodied interaction and in-situ behaviors, limiting realistic usability testing and user understanding of the deployed system.
reference_excerpt: The user study was conducted at a stationary terminal and not with the mobile robot as it was seldom available due to intensive technical system revisions.

description: Faulty person-tracking and orientation caused the robot to lose sight of customers and collide with objects, disrupting interactions.
justification: Persistent tracking and orientation malfunctions interfered with smooth guidance tours and human-robot dialogs, preventing reliable evaluation of interaction flows and hindering iterative adaptation to user needs.
reference_excerpt: the robot began to move away when interested customers were moving towards it (11 %, n = 4). The main reason for this problem was the not perfectly working person-tracking function. This defect also affected the guidance tour to the article positions in the home improvement store.

description: Environmental noise, announcements, dialects and unclear speech made reliable speech recognition infeasible, forcing a shift to menu-based touch interactions.
justification: The noisy, variable store context prevented designers from implementing and evaluating speech-based interaction, constraining design options and requiring alternative interface solutions that changed the scope of user-centred exploration.
reference_excerpt: Speech recognition is significantly more complex than other typical human-computer interaction scenarios due to (i) the extreme background noise in home stores, (ii) distracting public address announcements, (iii) the large diversity of descriptions for the same article... Therefore, it proved to be unrealistic to use speech recognition in order to identify desired articles.

description: Customers were unwilling to wear RFID tags, making RFID-based user detection impracticable.
justification: User reluctance to carry tags removed a potential tracking solution, constraining designers' ability to facilitate and evaluate reliable user detection approaches and forcing reliance on other sensing modalities.
reference_excerpt: Moreover, RFID proved as not practicable for user detection and tracking, because most customers are not willing to wear RFID tags.

description: Data collection used overt observation and oral interviews, exposing the design team to social desirability and investigator effects that may bias findings.
justification: Potential social desirability and investigator effects reduce the validity of user insights and thereby constrain designers' ability to accurately manage user understanding and to reliably evaluate and iterate designs.
reference_excerpt: Data collection was partly conducted by overt observations and oral interviews. Therefore, social desirability and investigator effects cannot be excluded.

description: Hardware energy limitations (battery life) forced removal of nonverbal features (blinking) because they drained the battery and increased recharging frequency.
justification: Energy constraints prevented sustaining embodied nonverbal behaviors, limiting designers' ability to produce and evaluate holistic social interaction features and iterate on robot personality/presentation.
reference_excerpt: Initially, the robot blinked during oral interactions with customers. However, when it was used often, blinking drained the battery very fast, leading to frequent recharging. Therefore, that feature was turned off.

description: The store environment is large, maze-like and highly dynamic (people, carts, changing shelf layouts), making robust mapping and navigation difficult.
justification: Environmental complexity constrained designers' ability to produce and evaluate reliable navigation and context-of-use models, increasing technical difficulty and limiting straightforward iterative improvements.
reference_excerpt: TOOMAS was implemented in a home improvement store, which is a very complex, maze-like indoor environment... The environment is highly dynamic due to moving people (customers, staff) or other moving objects like shopping carts.

description: Resource limitations prevented the ProACT platform from integrating all features required to fully support multimorbidity self-management (eg, medication management, care planning).
justification: Omitting these features constrained designers' ability to address holistic experience and to produce complete design solutions and user requirements for multimorbidity management.
reference_excerpt: First, given the resource limitations, the version of the ProACT platform described in this paper and evaluated in the trial did not integrate all of the features required to fully support the self-management of multimorbidity, with development initially focused on symptom and well-being monitoring, education, setting physical activity goals, and data sharing.

description: Project budget constraints limited triage staff and researcher availability to 9 AM–5 PM, Monday–Friday.
justification: Restricted support hours reduced the team's ability to facilitate user involvement and provide continuous evaluation/support, potentially limiting participants' engagement and the designers' capacity to gather feedback outside those hours.
reference_excerpt: The triage staff responded to alerts between 9 AM and 5 PM, Monday-Friday (hours were limited because of project budget) and made monthly check-in phone calls. Participants were made aware of the hours of triage...

description: Third-party device usability and reliability problems generated heavy technical support demand and caused some participants to withdraw from the trial.
justification: Device failures and mistrust in readings increased researchers' support workload and led to participant disengagement, which impeded the team's ability to evaluate the system with those users and to iterate based on their experiences.
reference_excerpt: Despite several reported device issues, participants felt that the platform was usable... 'It was just too hard to do because you couldn’t in the first place take the blood pressure anyway because it wasn’t working.' [P037, female, 82 years, COPD+CHD, Ireland]... Of these, 76 calls were requests for peripherals..., 121 were for devices not working..., 50 related to data syncing issues..., and 29 involved pairing or connection problems...

description: The SUS measure used did not distinguish usability between the CareApp and the symptom-monitoring devices.
justification: This measurement limitation reduced designers' ability to evaluate and specify separate user requirements or targeted improvements for the app versus the devices.
reference_excerpt: The SUS did not distinguish between the ProACT CareApp and symptom-monitoring devices. However, participant feedback suggests that the majority of usability issues lay with using the devices...

description: The proof-of-concept study design did not include a control group, preventing assessment of the effectiveness of individual platform components and services.
justification: Without a control group designers were unable to rigorously evaluate which features or services (eg, triage, technical support) were effective, limiting their ability to integrate feedback and iterate toward optimized solutions.
reference_excerpt: A further point with respect to the PoC study design ... is that a control group was not included; therefore, it was not possible to assess the effectiveness of individual components of the ProACT platform and related services (access to triage and technical support).

description: Helpdesk usage data were collected in Ireland but were not tracked in Belgium.
justification: Lack of comparable support data across countries limited the research team's ability to understand cross-site technical support needs and manage user understanding and involvement comprehensively.
reference_excerpt: To offer context to the necessity of the helpdesk, there were a total of 355 calls to the helpdesk in Ireland over the course of the trial (helpdesk calls were not tracked in Belgium).
